title: Large personal Atari ST, Amiga and DOS application/matching-game discovery
summary: Personally screen 563 candidate URLs and add 20 projects, with eight explicit non-promotion decisions.
notes: Root assistant personally searched 16 GitHub query routes plus a primary README relationship, screened 563 unique URLs and reviewed 28 repositories. Adds 20 game/application/library recoveries and records eight non-promotions. All four requested platforms searched; no new CPC game-source candidate qualified in this pass. Strong application coverage includes Atari ST PrintMaster, Amiga AMOS, VEDIT DOS reconstruction and M602 screensaver. Historical compiler/runtime reuse, relocation-normalized matching, symbolic assembly versus C progress, behavior-derived reimplementations and source-preservation variants are explicit. No upstream compiler, game, installer, screensaver, firmware or downloaded binary executed. Build flags remain unverified rather than converting upstream assertions into independent checks.

gamesrc-ver-recreation-raptor-readme-md.text:
Modified "Raptor: Call of the Shadows" sources with reconstructed DOS versions
==============================================================================

This source tree covers a modification of the open-source release
of Raptor: Call of the Shadows for DOS, with the main goal being
a reconstruction of sources matching multiple released binaries.

The original open-source release was made possible thanks to Scott Host of
Mountain King Studios. As a part of it, Nuke.YKT was reconstructing sources so
they'd match v1.2 as close as possible, while NY00123 was assisting with these
efforts. The modified source tree found here additionally covers reconstructed
sources for versions 1.0-1.1, mostly being worked on by Nuke.YKT again.

Technically speaking, there's the Raptor code under the SOURCE directory
and a support library found under the GFX directory. Another library
is required for sound output and other purposes.

In case you try making binaries from this codebase, the usual caveat is
that even with what appear to be the right tools, you might not get an exact
binary as it was released back in the days, for multiple technical reasons.

See orig-doc/README.md for the original open source release's notes as
written by skynettx, including description of license.

What is *not* included
----------------------

As in the case of the original open-source release, you won't find files from
the DMX library. They're still required for making the EXEs in such a way
that their layouts will be as close to the originals' as possible.

Alternatively, to make a functioning EXE consisting of GPL-compatible code
for the purpose of having a test playthrough, you can use a replacement.
One which may currently be used is the Apogee Sound System backed DMX wrapper,
i.e., APODMX. As expected, it'll sound different, especially the music.

List of covered versions
------------------------

With a few exceptions, using the right tools, this codebase can be used
for accurately recreating executables from shareware and registered
DOS versions 1.0, 1.1 and 1.2 of Raptor: Call of the Shadows.

List of releases by output directory names
------------------------------------------

These are the names used from the covered Raptor SOURCE tree:

- RAP10S: "Raptor: Call of the Shadows" Shareware v1.0.
- RAP10R: "Raptor: Call of the Shadows" Registered v1.0.
- RAP11S: "Raptor: Call of the Shadows" Shareware v1.1.
- RAP11R: "Raptor: Call of the Shadows" Registered v1.1.
- RAP12S: "Raptor: Call of the Shadows" Shareware v1.2.
- RAP12R: "Raptor: Call of the Shadows" Registered v1.2.

The included GFX tree uses these names: GFXRAP10, GFXRAP11 and GFXRAP12.

Technical details of the original EXEs (rather than any recreated one)
----------------------------------------------------------------------

|        Version        |  Bytes |               MD5                |  CRC-32  |
|-----------------------|--------|----------------------------------|----------|
|     Shareware 1.0     | 411441 | ee27ae538d34d5e68d76bc746aa2ea1e | b39d6e28 |
|    Registered 1.0     | 411445 | 8de63a2c2f396eaf53e9328488ec7f7d | 57c984a2 |
|     Shareware 1.1     | 437053 | 69a84ad0dbbae0683499dfb4a2f95996 | 0c212e59 |
|    Registered 1.1     | 437057 | e76369cbdd4eb2ad4284c80c2a38c356 | 8f4b620f |
|     Shareware 1.2     | 474343 | 3167a6c4b0f32d779319dd1639bb8702 | bad4de17 |
|    Registered 1.2     | 474359 | 0ade982eacb28ea4ea80c355b95dbbc5 | 7686d1c0 |

Prerequisites for building each EXE
-----------------------------------

Required tools:

- For versions of Raptor preceding 1.2 and the GFX library:
Watcom C 9.5b and no other version in the 9.5 series.
- For Raptor v1.2 (excluding GFX): Watcom C 10.0 and no other version.
- For all versions of Raptor and the GFX library: Turbo Assembler 3.1.

Additionally:

- As hinted earlier, GFX and Raptor originally made use of variations of DMX;
GFX itself (originally) bundled its own revision of a few DMX sources.
- Alternatively, if you want to get an EXE with entirely GPL-compatible
code, you can use the APODMX wrapper. In such a case,
the Apogee Sound System v1.09 will also be used.

Notes before trying to build anything:

- The EXEs will surely have great differences in layouts
without access to matching DMX files.
- Even with access to the correct versions of DMX, Watcom C and
Turbo Assembler, this may depend on luck. In fact, the compiler
may generate the contents of a function body a bit differently
if an additional environment variable is defined, or alternatively,
if a macro definition is added.
- Even if there are no such issues, certain versions of Watcom C
are known to insert data between C string literals, which appears to depend
on the environment, and/or the contents of the processed source codes.
This seems to be related to Watcom C 10.0b and earlier versions,
and less to 10.5, 10.6 or 11.0.
- The created RAP.EXE file will require an external DOS4GW.EXE file
or compatible. You may optionally use DOS/4GW Professional to bind
its loader to the EXE, but inspection of the EXE layout wasn't done.

Building any of the Raptor EXEs
-------------------------------

1. Make sure Watcom C 9.5b is appropriately set up,
and change to the GFX directory.
2. Use DOBUILD.BAT, selecting the GFX version matching the version of Raptor
that you're interested in building. In case you want to use the DMX wrapper,
enter "DOBUILD.BAT USE_APODMX".
3. If you want to build a Raptor v1.2 executable, start a new session
of DOS (or compatible), with Watcom C 10.0 being set up instead of 9.5b.
For earlier versions of Raptor, you may continue using the existing session.
4. Change to the SOURCE directory and use its own DOBUILD.BAT file to select
a version of Raptor to build. Enter "DOBUILD.BAT USE_APODMX" if you want
to use the DMX wrapper.
5. Hopefully you should get an EXE essentially behaving like the original,
with the possible exception of the DMX code.

rembish-color-lines-game-readme-md.text: # Color Lines (1992) — decompilation & multiplatform port «Color Lines» by Gamos (Moscow, 1992) — the game of every mom and dad in the 90s: a 9x9 board, balls of seven colours, three new ones after every move, and lines of five or more vanish. Programming Olga Demina, graphics Igor Ivkin & Gennady Denisov. This repo is a reverse-engineered port of `LINES.EXE` to portable C + SDL2: it runs natively and in a browser. **Play in the browser:** — with a global Top Ten. The page downloads the original's pictures for you from the Internet Archive (one click), or takes your own copy. [](https://github.com/rembish/color-lines-game/releases/download/v0.1.0/lines.mp4) *Click for the video with the PC speaker: the demo plays at a human's pace until the pretender passes the king's 100 points and takes his crown. Made with `tools/clips.sh` from your own copy of the game; the clips live in the releases, never in the repository.* The goal has two halves: 1. **Game logic: decompiled faithfully.** The Turbo Pascal random number generator and every call to it, where new balls land (and the probing that means the bottom-right cell is never drawn directly), the line check (a cross counts its centre once per direction), and the score, which depends on how long you thought about the move and is computed in Turbo Pascal's 6-byte Reals — reproduced bit for bit. 2. **Presentation: the original's own** pictures, read at run time from *your own copy* of `LINES.LIB`. Nothing of the original is in this repository. ## The original The tools in `re/` need your own copy of the DOS release in `original/` (git-ignored, never distributed): ``` bfa7f909c6360eb3a0586a43d44238f876e188788a7fc0cb2b7092a76ca13607 LINES.EXE e49c81cd16e4bf5253e4272a131c3f4817370f3f635923f36fb3b1e93a521f53 LINES.LIB ``` - Turbo Pascal with the Graph unit's EGA driver and Genus Microprogramming's PCX Toolkit; `LINES.LIB` is a "pcxLib" archive of five 16-colour PCX pictures (`re/tools/lines.py` extracts them). `Lines.res`, written by the game, holds the Top Ten. ## Playing Click a ball, then a free cell it can reach (or the arrow keys and Space). Five or more of one colour in a row — across, down or diagonal — vanish and score; otherwise the three balls shown under *Next* arrive. F1 help, F2 sound, F3 the next balls shown or not, F4 start again (the Top Ten all the same, as in the original), Esc the title, F11 full screen. On lines.rembi.sh every game is dealt by the server with a signed seed. At the end the browser sends the moves with the two clock readings of each; the server replays them with the same C core compiled to WebAssembly and books the score it gets itself (`cloudflare/`). Names are unique (the first browser to take one keeps it). Natively, and when the server does not answer, the Top Ten stays on this computer. ## Building ```sh cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build -j ./build/lines # looks for LINES.LIB in original/ or a folder you name make help # the everyday commands; `make check` is what CI runs tools/clips.sh 75 3 62 # the clip above (needs ffmpeg and original/) ``` Browser: `make web` (Emscripten; the web build and the server's core into `cloudflare/`), `node --test cloudflare/test.mjs` for the server. ## How faithful is it? - `re/emu/lemu.py` loads `LINES.EXE` into the Unicorn CPU emulator, stubs out only drawing, animation, sound, delays and the mouse, and runs the original's `play_game` with a scripted keyboard and a virtual clock. `re/emu/record.py` plays games with a bot (greedy lines, wasted reselects, unreachable targets, random and very long thinking times; games starting near midnight and at 18:12, where the original's clock arithmetic wraps; crafted boards with long lines and crosses; thinking times landing exactly on rounding ties) and checks the rules on every turn. - `tests/difftest.py` replays those games through `core/` and compares every turn: the board, the next colours, free cells, the score and the random seed; the moves the original refused must be refused too. `tests/real48.py` checks the 6-byte Real arithmetic against the original's own System routines on 50,000 random operands. `tests/mutants.py` breaks the core in 20 ways and checks that the difftest catches each. ```sh uv sync --extra dev .venv/bin/python re/emu/record.py 1 2 3 # games from the original (needs original/) cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build .venv/bin/python tests/difftest.py && .venv/bin/python tests/real48.py && .venv/bin/python tests/mutants.py ``` Findings and addresses are in [`re/NOTES.md`](re/NOTES.md). ## Code quality The core builds with `-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wshadow -Wconversion -Wsign-conversion` and more, clean under gcc and clang, and is kept clean under clang-tidy and clang-format 21; the Python tooling under ruff and `mypy --strict`. CI runs all of it on every push, with the sanitizers, the web build, the server's tests and three games recorded from the original (`tests/fixtures`); the deploy waits for it. ## Credits «Color Lines» © 1992 Gamos Ltd.: Olga Demina, Igor Ivkin, Gennady Denisov. This is an unofficial fan reimplementation for preservation; no original game files are distributed. The code of this port is under the [BSD 3-Clause License](LICENSE).

elthial-crescent-hawks-revenge-sdl-port-.text:
A readable C17 reconstruction of the 1990 DOS game.

This repository is a C17 reconstruction of the 1990 DOS game. Its purpose is preservation: express the executable's procedures, data flow, control flow and game rules as readable C while retaining a direct route back to the assembly. This repository starts at the consolidated v1.0 preservation snapshot. The monorepo's development commit history is intentionally not imported. This is not a redesign or the architecture for a future port. DOS, BIOS and hardware operations are redirected at the lowest practical boundary to SDL3 and portable host services; game logic remains in the reconstructed procedure chain. ## Current status Version 1.0 is supported and tested only on 64-bit Windows. The code is intended to remain portable, but other host platforms are not release-qualified. - All 785 known executable procedures are present in `src/Original`. - 588 procedures are `Verified` against assembly. - 197 procedures are `Verified [SDL]` at a documented platform boundary. - Two ledger rows are retained as non-procedure evidence. - No procedure remains `Unchecked` or partially verified. - All 785 procedures are validated in the readable reconstructed-C model. - The SDL Release suite contains 59 tests; the asset-independent headless suite contains 57. - Manual acceptance testing has completed the first six campaign missions. This establishes a functional preservation build, not proof that every campaign path or hardware nuance has been exercised. See [`docs/CAMPAIGN_SMOKE_TEST.md`](docs/CAMPAIGN_SMOKE_TEST.md) for the acceptance record and current limits.

## Quick start Requirements: - Windows with Visual Studio C/C++ build tools; - PowerShell; - CMake and Ninja supplied by Visual Studio; - SDL3 for the playable build; and - a legally obtained copy of the original game data. Run the asset-independent build and tests: ```powershell ./Build.ps1 -Headless -Configuration Release ``` For local play, put the original game files in `assets/original-game` and run: ```powershell ./Run-Revenge.ps1 ``` Or use an installation elsewhere: ```powershell ./Run-Revenge.ps1 -OriginalAssetDirectory ../Chrevenge ``` The launcher builds `Revenge`, checks for `MEDIA.CFG`, prevents accidental multiple instances and supplies the asset location without copying the game. Use `-NoBuild` to run an existing executable and `-Trace` for host-boundary diagnostics. ## Minimal runtime package Create a distributable runtime shell with: ```powershell ./Build.ps1 -Configuration Release -Package ``` `build-release/package` contains exactly: ```text Revenge.exe REVENGE.CFG ``` The package deliberately contains no copyrighted game data. `build-release/Revenge-1.0.0-SHA256SUMS.txt` records the SHA-256 of both package files and is intentionally kept beside the package directory. `REVENGE.CFG` locates the user's original installation: ```ini asset_directory=. ``` The default permits the two files to be copied into an original installation. SDL3 is statically linked into `Revenge.exe`, fixing each release to the SDL version with which it was built and avoiding a separate runtime DLL. A relative or absolute path may instead keep program and data separate. `REVENGE_ASSET_DIRECTORY` overrides the configuration for launchers and test environments. ## Preservation model | Area | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | `src/Original` | Reconstructed executable procedures and typed executable-owned data | | `src/Support` | Host representation bridges with no claimed original procedure boundary | | `src/SDL` | SDL3 and operating-system implementations below original DOS/hardware wrappers | | `include` | Shared C interfaces and packed data contracts | | `evidence` | Self-contained annotations, metadata, assembly and research records | | `docs/METHOD_TABLE.csv` | Address-keyed behavioral verification ledger | | `docs/SOURCE_CONVERSION_TABLE.csv` | Address-keyed readable-C conversion ledger | | `tests` | Focused behavior, boundary and preservation checks | | `tools` | Ledger, evidence and package validation utilities | The governing rules are in [`docs/PRESERVATION_PLAN.md`](docs/PRESERVATION_PLAN.md). The reconstructed source model is described in [`docs/RECONSTRUCTED_C_PLAN.md`](docs/RECONSTRUCTED_C_PLAN.md). The [`documentation guide`](docs/README.md) distinguishes current policy from historical audit records. Supported DOS executable hashes are recorded in [`docs/SUPPORTED_VERSIONS.md`](docs/SUPPORTED_VERSIONS.md). Contributions must follow [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md), particularly the original-bug and SDL-boundary rules. Release changes are in [`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md). ## Verification and diagnostics `tools/Test-PreservationLedgers.ps1` checks paths, address/name uniqueness, aliases, final verification states, addressless helpers and direct SDL access from `src/Original`. Passing tests are regression evidence; the assembly and observed original behavior remain authoritative. Normal builds exclude diagnostics injected into reconstructed procedure bodies. For an explicitly instrumented investigation: ```powershell ./Build.ps1 -Configuration Release -PreservationInstrumentation ./Run-Revenge.ps1 -NoBuild -Trace -OriginalAssetDirectory ../Chrevenge ``` Injected observations use `REVENGE_PRESERVATION_TRACE` so they remain visibly separate from the reconstructed logic. ## Known limits - The complete campaign has not been acceptance-tested. - Presentation and audio are functional but are not cycle- or waveform-identical to DOS hardware. - Stored 16:16 addresses and interrupt-era behavior still require host representation bridges where their numeric form is observable. - Original assets are required for normal play and are not distributed here. ## Rights and licensing Project-authored code and excluded reconstructed or third-party material are described in [`LICENSE`](LICENSE), [`LICENSES/README.md`](LICENSES/README.md), [`NOTICE.md`](NOTICE.md), and [`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). The original executable, raw game assets, saves and extracted asset dumps are not included. The limited documentation images are covered by `NOTICE.md`. This is an independent preservation and research project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the game's publishers or the owners of BattleTech.

joeshaw-sre-reconstructed-readme-md.text: # Solar Realms Elite, reconstructed [Solar Realms Elite](http://www-cs-students.stanford.edu/~amitp/Articles/SRE-Documentation.html) (SRE) is a 1990s [BBS door game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBS_door) by Amit Patel. In SRE, players each build an empire in one shared galaxy, a few turns a day. The game's source code was lost in 1996. This repository is a C++ reconstruction of the last release, 0.994b (March 7, 1995), made by reverse engineering `SRE.EXE`. It builds on macOS and Linux and plays in a terminal. There is also a Rust port in the [`rust` branch](https://github.com/joeshaw/sre-reconstructed/tree/rust). The reverse engineering and implementation was done using Claude Code and the Opus 5.5 model over the course of about a day. [You can play it online here.](https://solar-realms.exe.xyz/) ![The empire status screen](docs/screenshot.png) The goal is to behave exactly like the original: the same screens, prompts, colors, and numbers, the same random events, and game files the original can read. The tests check this by running the original in an emulator alongside the reconstruction, giving both the same input, and comparing the results (see [Testing](#testing)). To see how it was reverse engineered with Claude Code, see [How it was made](#how-it-was-made). ## Getting started You need `make` and a C++ compiler: the Xcode command line tools on macOS (`xcode-select --install`), or `build-essential` on Debian and Ubuntu. git clone https://github.com/joeshaw/sre-reconstructed cd sre-reconstructed make tools/newgame.sh ~/sre "Your Name" SRE_DIR=~/sre ./sre reset # once, as the sysop SRE_DIR=~/sre ./sre # play `make` builds `./sre`. `tools/newgame.sh` copies the original release's data files (help text, screens, flavors, and the research table) from `game/` into a new game directory, and writes a door file for you. The first time, `sre reset` asks for the sysop's name and the BBS name, then opens the sysop menu. The sysop is the person who runs the BBS and the game. Choose **2** (Reset the Game), name the galaxy, and press Enter to accept the default for each setting. Then press **Q** to leave. If `sre` exits without printing anything, the game hasn't been set up yet, so run `sre reset` first. The game's own help explains how to play. The original's documentation is in [`game/DOCS/`](game/DOCS), and Amit Patel has also posted [documentation](http://www-cs-students.stanford.edu/~amitp/Articles/SRE-Documentation.html) and [notes on the game's design](http://www-cs-students.stanford.edu/~amitp/Articles/SRE-Design.html) on his web site. ## What is reconstructed All of the game is reconstructed: joining, turns, the economy, food, population, the spending, selling, and planet menus, operations, covert operations, attacks of every kind, pirates, trading fleets, diplomacy, messages, news, the lottery, the bank, bonds, investments, events, research, maintenance, scores, the sysop menu and its editors, resources, translations, and flavors. Some parts belong to the BBS and DOS rather than the game, and are left out: the serial port and FOSSIL drivers, the sysop's status bars and hot keys on the local screen, sysop chat, EMS and XMS memory swapping, and the VGA palette. The terminal stands in for the caller's modem. In a local session (`sre sysop`, `sre reset`, or local play), it also stands in for the sysop's screen and keyboard. The game is always registered, so it has everything registration added to the original: the bank, bonds, investments, the Super Daily lottery, nuclear, chemical, and psionic weapons, and the full reset options. The registered name and the bank's name come from `STATUS.SRE` if there is one, without checking its key. Otherwise the game is registered to the sysop. The original only accepts dates up to December 11, 1999, so the reconstruction moves the clock back 44 years (see `SRE_DATE_SHIFT` below). ## Playing `sre sysop` opens the sysop menu again after the first reset: the empire viewer, the player and pirate editors, and messages. Commands are not case sensitive. Other players can share the game directory. As on a BBS, only one person can play at a time. Before each one plays, change the first line of `DOORFILE.SR` to their name. ### The door file The BBS used `DOORFILE.SR` to tell SRE about the caller. It has eight lines, and the game reads the first seven: Your Name the user's name on the BBS 1 ANSI color (1/0) 1 IBM (PC) characters (1/0) 25 lines on the screen 38400 baud rate 1 COM port; 0 for a local (sysop) session 60 minutes left Your Name the user's real name `tools/newgame.sh` fills in the terminal's height, and the name defaults to `$USER`. ### Settings Settings in `RESOURCE.DAT` work as described in the original's [`DOCS/RESOURCE.DOC`](game/DOCS/RESOURCE.DOC), except those for the parts left out (serial ports, FOSSIL, display, status bars, and swapping), which are ignored. On the command line, on/off settings can be given as `/Name`, `/NoName`, or `/Name=Y` (or `-` instead of `/`). The original's documents use the IBM PC character set, so their box drawings look garbled on GitHub. Environment variables: - `SRE_DIR`: the game directory (default: the current directory). - `SRE_CHARSET`: `utf8` or `cp437`. The game's text uses the IBM PC character set. When this is unset, the game converts it to UTF-8 if its output is a terminal and the locale is UTF-8 (the default on macOS). - `SRE_DATE_SHIFT`: years to move the clock back (default 44). The original only accepts dates from December 25, 1979 to December 11, 1999. A shift of 44 years works from 2024 until December 11, 2043, and keeps leap years lined up because it is a multiple of 4. (The weekdays don't line up, but the game never shows them.) Use another multiple of 4 after that, and don't change it during a game: a game's dates are stored shifted. Past the limit, `sre` exits without printing anything. ## Running it on the web `server/` contains `sre-server`, which runs the game the way a BBS ran a door: one shared game and one player at a time, each playing in a terminal in their browser on a page styled like a BBS. It needs Go (see `server/go.mod` for the version): make sre server tools/newgame.sh ~/sre-web/game server/sre-server -listen :8000 -game ~/sre-web/game -sre ./sre \ -keys ~/sre-web/keys.json -sysops YourName Browsers only allow the page's login keys over HTTPS (or on `localhost`), so serve it behind a proxy that handles TLS, such as Caddy or nginx. [`server/README.md`](server/README.md) has more details, including how to run it on exe.dev. ## Testing `tests/smoke.sh` requires Python 3.7 or later. It sets up a game from `game/`, resets it, joins two players, plays turns, and runs the next day's maintenance. Then it compares the output and the game's data with the recordings in `tests/smoke/`, which match the original's byte for byte. CI runs this test on macOS and Linux. make && tests/smoke.sh The full tests compare against the original. `tools/dosemu.py` (see [How it was made](#how-it-was-made)) runs the original `SRE.EXE`, and the reconstruction runs on a copy of the same game with the same input. The tests compare the output byte for byte, the game's files after decrypting them (leaving out the bytes the original never initializes), and the random number sequence. They need `curl`, `unzip`, and Python with [Unicorn](https://www.unicorn-engine.org/): python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate pip install unicorn pyte capstone # pyte for tools/render.py, capstone for tools/disasm.py tests/fixtures.sh /tmp/srefix # games made by the original, some with fields edited tests/run.sh /tmp/srefix # the scenarios in tests/scenarios.txt tests/fuzz.sh /tmp/srefix army 1 20 # random play, seeds 1 to 20 tests/fuzzchain.sh /tmp/srefix two 1 # two players taking turns over several days `tests/fixtures.sh` downloads the original release, `sre0994b.zip`, from [John Dailey Software](https://www.johndaileysoftware.com/), verifies its SHA-256 checksum, and runs the `SRE.EXE` inside it to create the games that the scenarios start from. You can also give it the zip: `tests/fixtures.sh DIR path/to/sre0994b.zip`. The tests run with `SRE_UNREGISTERED` set, so registration works as in the original: the game is unregistered unless there is a valid `STATUS.SRE`. If you have one from a registered copy of the original, set `SRE_STATUS=path/to/STATUS.SRE` and `tests/fixtures.sh` also makes registered games for the bank, bond, and lottery scenarios. Without it, `tests/run.sh` skips those scenarios. `SRE_CLOCK` gives the tests a frozen clock, in seconds since 1970. It is read as local time and is not shifted, so it must be a date the original accepts. ## How it was made Claude Opus 5.5 running inside Claude Code reconstructed the game. Here is my original prompt in an empty repository: > solar realms elite was a bbs door from the 90s. the source code was lost > in 1996. > > i want you to reverse engineer the last release (available at > https://www.johndaileysoftware.com/download/?method=2&terms=1) from the > binary and produce source code we can compile on a modern mac. it is not > necessary to reconstruct the BBS/fossil parts, but the gameplay and text > user interface need to be reconstructed perfectly from the original. > > Additional info from the original author can be found on > http://www-cs-students.stanford.edu/~amitp/Articles/SRE-Design.html and > other pages on his site. > > Use this repository to build it The work went in five steps. 1. Taking the binary apart. `SRE.EXE` is a Borland C++ large-model program, and most of its code is in VROOMM overlays, Borland's system for loading parts of a program from the `.EXE` only when they are needed. `tools/deoverlay.py` turns it into a plain executable with every segment in place, so it can be disassembled as a whole. Ghidra produced the function list and call graph in `tools/re/`. `tools/disasm.py`, built on [Capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/), produces listings annotated with names and strings, and `tools/vtables.py` finds the virtual tables. `tools/lift.py`, a pseudo-C lifter for Borland's code, makes the listings easier to read. 2. Running the original. `tools/dosemu.py` emulates just enough of DOS, the BIOS, and a FOSSIL driver, on top of [Unicorn](https://www.unicorn-engine.org/), to run `SRE.EXE` with scripted input on its serial line or keyboard and a frozen clock. It captures the game's output, screen, and files. With it, any question about how the original behaves can be answered by running it. 3. Writing the source. Each part of the original was rewritten in turn in C++, keeping the original's structure: one file per part of the program (usually one code segment), the original's classes (streams, menus, and the objects stored in the data files), and each function's address in a comment, in the 16-bit `segment:offset` form, so it can be found in the original binary. Where the game depends on how the Borland runtime and compiler behave, that behavior is reproduced exactly: the random number generator, the date and time conversions, the `ctype` table, text-mode file reads, and 16-bit integer arithmetic. 4. Checking it. Each part was checked by running it and the original on copies of the same game with the same input, and comparing the output, the game's files, and the random number sequence (observed through the encryption salts it produces). The scenarios in `tests/scenarios.txt` go through the menus and features, and random play (`tests/fuzz.sh`, and `tests/fuzzchain.sh` for several players over multiple days) found what the scenarios missed. The registered features were checked with a registration file, which is not included here. 5. Naming. At first, names came from the disassembly, such as `d188` for the field at that offset in a record. Once everything worked, each name was replaced with one based on how the game uses it (`pollution`), and the tests confirmed that nothing changed. ## Repository layout - `src/`: the reconstructed game, with the original's addresses in the comments. - `game/`: the original release's data files and documentation. - `server/`: `sre-server`, the web front end. - `tests/`: the smoke test and its recordings, the scenarios, and the scripts that compare with the original. - `tools/`: helpers for comparing runs (`difftest.sh`, `localtest.sh`, `render.py`, `localdiff.py`, `memdiff.py`, `playercmp.py`, and `streamcmp.py`), for setting up and editing games (`newgame.sh`, `sredata.py`, and `sreedit.py`), and for reverse engineering (`deoverlay.py`, `disasm.py`, `lift.py`, `vtables.py`, and `dosemu.py`). - `tools/re/`: Ghidra's list of the original's functions (address, size, callers, and callees). `names.txt` gives names to about 120 of them, the ones identified first (the Borland runtime, streams, files, resources, and strings), and `tools/disasm.py` and `tools/lift.py` show calls to them by name. `globals.txt` is for names of data addresses, and is empty. ## Rust port The `rust` branch has the same game ported to Rust, module by module from the C++. Its output and files are byte for byte the same as the C++ build's, and so the original's, in every scenario and in thousands of random games. It needs only Rust and Cargo (`git checkout rust`, then `make`), and has no dependencies beyond `libc`. ## License Well, this is a bit complicated. The original game (in `game/`) is Copyright 1992-1995 by Amit J Patel. The game was distributed on BBSes as shareware. From the documentation: ``` Registration is NOT required to run SRE. SRE might be classified as one of these types of programs: Shareware - Yes! SRE is shareware. You are required to register this game after 99 years of trial use! Freeware - Yes! SRE could be considered freeware. (However, freeware is a trademarked term.) You are not required to pay any fee for this program. However, we do give benefits to those who donate $15 or more. Crippleware - Yes! SRE is slightly crippled! You can't access the bank in the unregistered version. (But you don't need the bank to play the game.) Bogusware - Yes! SRE is bogusware! It will destroy itself after 99 years! (If you don't register!) (just kidding!) Deadware - Yes! You must've found the bugs! Bonusware - Yes! If you register, you get bonuses (like the bank)! (I prefer to think of it as Bonusware.) ``` The reconstructed source code (in `src/`) is clearly a derivative work of the original game. It is being distributed with Amit Patel's permission. To the extent that human-prompted agent-developed software is copyrightable, the reconstructed source, tools, server and tests are Copyright 2026 Joe Shaw and licensed under the MIT license: > Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining a copy > of this software and associated documentation files (the "Software"), to deal > in the Software without restriction, including without limitation the rights > to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell > copies of the Software, and to permit persons to whom the Software is > furnished to do so, subject to the following conditions: > > The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all > copies or substantial portions of the Software. > > THE SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED "AS IS", WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, EXPRESS OR > IMPLIED, INCLUDING BUT NOT LIMITED TO THE WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY, FITNESS > FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE AND NONINFRINGEMENT. IN NO EVENT SHALL THE AUTHORS OR > COPYRIGHT HOLDERS BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM, DAMAGES OR OTHER LIABILITY, WHETHER IN > AN ACTION OF CONTRACT, TORT OR OTHERWISE, ARISING FROM, OUT OF OR IN CONNECTION > WITH THE SOFTWARE OR THE USE OR OTHER DEALINGS IN THE SOFTWARE. The server includes xterm.js which is licensed under the xterm license. See `server/web/vendor/XTERM-LICENSE`. ## Credits Solar Realms Elite was written by Amit Patel, now of [Red Blob Games](https://www.redblobgames.com/). The reconstruction relies on [Ghidra](https://ghidra-sre.org/), [Capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/), and [Unicorn](https://www.unicorn-engine.org/), and the web front end includes [xterm.js](https://xtermjs.org/).

nrnelson-watcom-c-6-5-restoration-readme.text:
# Watcom C 6.5 run-time library restoration

Watcom C 6.5, released in 1988, is, as far as I have been able to find,
the earliest version of the Watcom C compiler that still survives.  The
only copy of it I could find is damaged: its small-model and compact-model
run-time libraries, `CLIBS.LIB` and `CLIBC.LIB`, have each lost more than
half of their contents.  Without them the compiler can only build medium,
large and huge model programs.  Another copy may well exist somewhere (see
[below](#looking-for-another-copy)); until one turns up, this restoration
is the way to make the compiler whole again.

This repository rebuilds the two libraries from what survives, documents
every step, and lets anyone repeat the restoration from the original
archive with one command, on Linux or Windows.

**The restored libraries are reconstructions, not the originals.**
Without an undamaged copy of the files, or a checksum of them, the result
cannot be proven identical to what Watcom shipped.  Everything that survived is kept
byte for byte; everything rebuilt is labelled, module by module, with how
it was made and how confident the reconstruction is.


## Why this matters

Watcom grew out of the University of Waterloo, and its C compiler became one of the most
respected optimising compilers of the DOS era.  Its code generator shaped
a generation of PC software, its descendants were used to build classics
such as *DOOM*, and its source was eventually released as Open Watcom,
which is still maintained today.  Version 6.5 is, as far as I can tell,
where the surviving record of that line begins: I have not been able to
find a copy of 6.0 or anything earlier, though that does not mean none
exists.

Software from this period disappears quietly.  Floppy disks fail, hard
disks are thrown away, companies change hands, and the people who wrote
the code retire.  When the last copy of a program is damaged, the damage
becomes the history unless someone repairs it.  A compiler is a
particularly important thing to keep working: it is the key to the
software written with it, to the documentation and articles that describe
it, and to understanding how programmers of the time actually worked.

The surviving copy of Watcom C 6.5 sits in the public
[Watcom C/C++ Compilers collection](https://archive.org/details/watcom-c-cpp-compilers-collection)
on the Internet Archive, the only copy I could find.  Anyone who
downloads it today gets a compiler
that cannot build small or compact model programs (the small model was
the one most DOS programs of the time used), and that fails in confusing
ways if they try.
This project exists so that the compiler can be used again as it was
meant to be, and so that the method, the evidence and its limits are on
record for anyone who comes later.


## What was wrong with the surviving copy

The archive holds the eight distribution disks of Watcom C 6.5 as plain
files (DISK1-DISK8), dated 31 May 1988.  Every file checks out except two:

| library | model | state in the archive |
|---|---|---|
| `CLIBS.LIB` | small (near code, near data) | 96 of 188 sectors replaced, 141 of 250 modules lost |
| `CLIBC.LIB` | compact (near code, far data) | 101 of 198 sectors replaced, 146 of 250 modules lost |
| `CLIBM.LIB`, `CLIBL.LIB`, `CLIBH.LIB` | medium, large, huge | intact |

Whole 512-byte sectors of the two files hold other files' data instead:
pieces of `WDISASM.EXE`, `WMAKE.EXE`, `WLINK.EXE`, `WVIDEO.HLP`,
`MATHM.LIB` and `CLIBM.LIB`, mostly at the same offsets those files have
themselves.  It looks like the copy was made from a hard disk with
unreadable sectors, where the copying tool left whatever it had read
before.  The true bytes of those sectors are gone; a checksum can show a
record is bad, but cannot bring back its content.  Three further bytes in
otherwise good sectors are corrupted by bit errors.

What did survive is still a great deal: each library's dictionary is
intact (so the name, position and size of every lost module is known),
106 and 102 modules survive whole, and the medium, large and huge
libraries, built from the same sources, are complete.

### Looking for another copy

Before starting, I looked for another copy, without success:

- The Internet Archive collection above holds only this one copy of 6.5;
  its "7.0" is WATCOM C 386 7.0, the 32-bit protected-mode edition, which
  has no 16-bit libraries at all.
- Later versions (8.x to 11.0) have a different code generator and
  run-time library, so they cannot supply 6.5's bytes.
- The WATCOM Express C library shipped with 6.5 is the medium-model
  library plus Express's own modules: no small-model code.
- I could not find any copy of 6.0 or earlier either.

That is the limit of my search, not proof that nothing else survives.
Copies of software like this turn up in attics, old office storage and
private collections, and there may well be another 6.5, or a 6.0,
somewhere.  If you have original Watcom C disks, or a copy of `CLIBS.LIB`
or `CLIBC.LIB` from them, please get in touch: a genuine copy would let
every reconstructed module here be checked, and would itself be worth
preserving.


## How the libraries were rebuilt

In short (the full account, with the evidence for every rule, the
decisions taken and the hypotheses that failed, is in
[METHOD.md](METHOD.md)):

1. **Map the damage** sector by sector, and find which modules survive
   whole, in part, or not at all.
2. **Learn exactly how the libraries were built**, by compiling small test
   programs with Watcom C 6.5 itself (it is intact) in every memory model.
3. **Convert**: a small-model module differs from its medium-model twin
   only in how code is addressed (near instead of far), and a compact one
   from its large twin the same way.  A converter turns medium and large
   modules into small and compact ones: calls, returns, stack frames,
   jumps, relocations, and the exact way the compiler splits and orders
   its object records, all recovered from the surviving modules.
4. **Recompile** where conversion is not enough (modules that handle
   pointers to functions): C source was reconstructed by reading the
   machine code, until Watcom C 6.5 compiled it to exactly the bytes of the
   intact medium and large libraries; the same source is then compiled for
   small and compact.
5. **Assemble** both libraries with every module at its original position,
   filling exactly its original space, matching every surviving byte, and
   naming exactly the symbols the original dictionary lists.
6. **Test** real programs built in all four models and compare their
   output.

Every rule was tested on the modules that survived before it was used on
the ones that were lost.


## Results

| | CLIBS.LIB (small) | CLIBC.LIB (compact) |
|---|---|---|
| original modules, kept byte for byte | 106 (+1 repaired) | 102 |
| rebuilt and matching every surviving byte of a partly damaged module | 2 | 2 |
| rebuilt with nothing left to check against | 141 | 146 |

- On the modules that survived, the converter reproduces 97 of 106 small
  and 93 of 102 compact modules byte for byte, every record; the
  recompile route reproduces the one module it was tested on (PRINTF) in
  all five libraries, including the surviving small and compact ones.
- The partly surviving compact `SCNF` module, 3088 of its 3424 bytes
  intact, is matched exactly by the rebuilt one.
- Both restored libraries pass a strict check of every module and record,
  link with Watcom's own linker, and the test programs (strings, stdio,
  floating point, files, directories, time, setjmp, signals, three kinds
  of heap, environment, spawn and exec) give the same output in all four
  memory models.
- **Confidence**: an estimated 90-94% of all modules are byte-identical to
  the lost originals, and 97-98% of all bytes; the chance that either whole
  library is byte-identical is close to zero.  Behaviour is better than
  that: everything tested works as the originals do.

`PROVENANCE.csv` lists every module of both libraries: whether it is
original or rebuilt, how, with what confidence, and anything unusual the
tools noted about it.


## Restoring the libraries yourself

The repository contains no Watcom files.  You need the original archive,
Python and DOSBox-X; the script does the rest.  Nothing outside the
repository folder is written.

### 1. Get the original archive

Download **`Watcom C.ver.6.5.English.zip`** from the Internet Archive:

- collection page: <https://archive.org/details/watcom-c-cpp-compilers-collection>
- direct download:
  <https://archive.org/download/watcom-c-cpp-compilers-collection/watcom-6.5/Watcom%20C.ver.6.5.English.zip>

and put it in the repository folder (or give its path to the script).  It
must be exactly this file; the script checks it:

| | |
|---|---|
| size | 1,286,189 bytes |
| SHA-256 | `76b2ebc8ec730ee1151b1c1f9193460b8cfc03dacec5d567573296f3a537eca6` |
| SHA-1 | `dc1547755776922145461010f99077fdcc35f770` |
| MD5 | `0ee269bc6e38a1ca2a3aab7ec9b9bf0d` |

### 2. Install the requirements

- **Python 3.8 or later.**
- **DOSBox-X** (any recent version).  It runs Watcom C 6.5's own compiler
  and linker, which are DOS programs.

Tested on Linux (Python 3.13, DOSBox-X 2025.02.01) and Windows (Python
3.12, DOSBox-X 2026.10.01): the same result, byte for byte, on both.

**Linux** (Debian/Ubuntu shown; use your distribution's packages or the
DOSBox-X Flatpak):

```
sudo apt install python3 dosbox-x
```

**Windows**: install Python from <https://www.python.org/downloads/>
(tick "Add python.exe to PATH"), and DOSBox-X from
<https://dosbox-x.com/> (the installer, or the portable zip).  The script
finds DOSBox-X on the PATH or in `C:\DOSBox-X` and `C:\Program Files\DOSBox-X`;
anywhere else, tell it where:

```
set WCR_DOSBOX=D:\Tools\DOSBox-X\dosbox-x.exe
```

**macOS**: Python from python.org or Homebrew, DOSBox-X from
<https://dosbox-x.com/>; set `WCR_DOSBOX` to the `dosbox-x` binary inside
the app bundle if it is not on the PATH.

### 3. Run the restoration

Linux and macOS:

```
git clone https://github.com/nrnelson/watcom-c-6.5-restoration.git
cd watcom-c-6.5-restoration
cp ~/Downloads/"Watcom C.ver.6.5.English.zip" .
python3 restore.py
```

Windows (Command Prompt or PowerShell):

```
git clone https://github.com/nrnelson/watcom-c-6.5-restoration.git
cd watcom-c-6.5-restoration
copy "%USERPROFILE%\Downloads\Watcom C.ver.6.5.English.zip" .
py restore.py
```

(Without git, download the repository as a zip from GitHub's green
**Code** button and unpack it.)

It takes about a minute.  It checks the archive, installs Watcom C 6.5 into
`build/watcom` the way its own installer would, compiles the four
reconstructed modules with Watcom C 6.5 in DOSBox-X (no window opens),
rebuilds both libraries into `out/`, checks every module and record, and
compares the result with the published restoration.  It ends with:

```
out/CLIBS.LIB: 250 modules ok
  SHA-256 95100563d6885e7f0eba7c1a96aa0587bdf2fbe9ef8bfbaf73a367f85216b8c0: identical to the published restoration
out/CLIBC.LIB: 250 modules ok
  SHA-256 b53e05b77252a952e0896abc3612846bae2a10f4c584d1fa682e752b6e24bcae: identical to the published restoration
```

The process is deterministic: the same archive gives the same bytes on
every machine.  Add `--test` to also build and run the test programs in
all four memory models (a few more minutes).

### 4. Use them

`out/CLIBS.LIB` and `out/CLIBC.LIB` replace the damaged files in the `LIB`
directory of a Watcom C 6.5 installation (in DOS, an emulator, or a
virtual machine).  The script can do it, keeping the damaged files as
`CLIBS.BAD` and `CLIBC.BAD`:

```
python3 restore.py --install /path/to/WATCOM/LIB
```

`build/watcom` is itself a complete Watcom C 6.5 installation, unpacked
from the archive, if you do not have one.


## What is in this repository

| | |
|---|---|
| `restore.py` | the whole restoration in one command |
| `tools/` | the tools it uses, each runnable alone (listed in METHOD.md) |
| `recompile/` | the reconstructed C sources and their compiler switches |
| `tests/` | the test programs |
| `METHOD.md` | the complete method: every rule, its evidence, every decision |
| `PROVENANCE.csv` | the result for every module of both libraries |

Made when you run it, and not committed: `build/` (the installed compiler
and work files) and `out/` (the restored libraries).


## Limits

- For 141 small and 146 compact modules nothing survives to check the
  reconstruction against.  On surviving modules the methods are about 91%
  exact (conversion) and exact in every tested case (recompilation and the
  small/compact cross check); the kinds of module where they are weakest
  are known and marked low in `PROVENANCE.csv`.
- A few decisions had to be made where the evidence ran out; each is
  explained in METHOD.md, section 11, with its alternative.
- Some original sources contained small-model-only code that no other
  library can reveal; for lost modules such differences cannot be seen.


## Rights

Watcom C is a product of Watcom Systems Inc.; its rights passed to Sybase
and then SAP.  This repository contains none of Watcom's files or code:
the tools read your own copy of the archive, and the restored libraries
are produced on your machine.  The restored libraries are derived from
Watcom's and remain subject to Watcom's (now SAP's) rights; they are not
distributed here.  The tools, tests, documentation and reconstructed
sources are © 2026 Nathan Nelson, released under the MIT licence
(`LICENSE`); the licence covers only that work, not Watcom's.

Open Watcom (<https://github.com/open-watcom/open-watcom-v2>) is the open
source descendant of Watcom C/C++ and is unrelated to this work.

lemiur-alien-trilogy-decomp-readme-md.text:
# Alien Trilogy (PS1) matching decompilation

A reconstruction of the C source of *Alien Trilogy* (Probe Entertainment / Acclaim, 1996) for
the PlayStation, USA release (`SLUS_000.07`). The source is written so that the game's original
compiler, with its original flags, turns it back into the exact bytes of the retail executable,
function by function. The aim is readable code with real names and types; a byte match is the
proof that the reconstruction is faithful, not the end goal.

This repository contains no game data and no Sony or SN Systems software (see
[Requirements](#requirements)).

Note that this was done with an obscene amount of AI assistance. I've done my best to keep code 
quality at a readable level, but there's some stuff here that's pretty clumsy. I'm releasing this
in the hopes that I can find people interested in collaborating to improve the code readability and
help ensure naming accuracy. 

## Target

| | |
|---|---|
| Executable | `SLUS_000.07`, PS-X EXE, 516,096 bytes (2,048-byte header + 514,048-byte payload) |
| SHA-256 | `f424660920764ac70f697b5b909a42fe259a76e60acbf5b01c6ca3ee8c8f8e98` |
| Load address / entry / GP | `0x80010000` / `0x800588c4` / `0x8008cd74` |
| Compiler | GCC 2.5.7 (PsyQ `CC1PSX`), `-O2 -G8` |
| Assembler | ASPSX 2.34 (ASPSX 2.08 and GNU as for a few library modules) |
| Libraries | Sony Runtime Library 3.3 |

## Progress

Every figure below comes from the byte gate (`tools/gate.py`), which links everything built
from this repository over the original executable and records where each payload byte came
from. The current tree passes:

```
GATE OK sha256=f424660920764ac70f697b5b909a42fe259a76e60acbf5b01c6ca3ee8c8f8e98 source_bytes=254030/514048 verbatim_bytes=0 generated_bytes=8079 asm_bytes=63848 library_asm_bytes=50237 units=75
```

| Category | Count | Bytes | Payload |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Game C functions | 645 functions | 205,436 | 39.96% |
| Game C initialized data | 287 definitions | 40,515 | 7.88% |
| Compiler-generated data of the C units (string pools, constants) | 406 items | 8,079 | 1.57% |
| **Decompiled game C** (gate `source_bytes`) | | **254,030** | **49.42%** |
| Hand-written GTE/renderer assembly | 32 routines + 312 tables | 63,848 | 12.42% |
| Sony library modules rebuilt as assembly (no archived match) | 153 routines + 184 data | 50,237 | 9.77% |
| Sony Runtime Library 3.3, identified against the SDK (text) | 96 modules | 27,796 | 5.41% |
| Sony Runtime Library 3.3, identified against the SDK (data) | 33 sections | 100,949 | 19.64% |
| Not yet accounted for | 452 gaps | 17,188 | 3.34% |
| **Total** | | **514,048** | 100% |

About half of the executable is now compiled from reconstructed C. Almost all of the rest is
either hand-written assembly or Sony's own libraries, which are identified but not
decompiled. The remaining 17 KB is in 452 gaps; 427 of them are 4 bytes or fewer, and 17
larger gaps of up to 1.9 KB hold most of the bytes.

A byte match alone does not make a function finished. **637 of the 645 byte-matched functions
are also matched under the project's code rules** (`tools/rules.py`): no fake code, no raw
offset access, declarations in their owning headers, no placeholder steering. The other 8 are
marked `MATCH-PENDING`: their bytes are exact, but the source still relies on a construct the
rules reject, and each carries a note saying what has been tried.

`PROGRESS.md` holds the same table as generated by `tools/progress.py`, which cross-checks the
gate's record against an independent per-function comparison and fails if they disagree.

## What has been decompiled

35 C units (about 29,000 lines), grouped by subsystem:

- **Core:** `main` (boot and the main loop), `tasker` (the cooperative task system),
  `geometry`, `text`, `sprites`, `texture_upload`, `movie`
- **Gameplay:** `player`, `actor` (aliens, colonists and their AI and animation),
  `weapon_slots`, `particle`, `particle_hits`, `debris`, `effects`, `lights`, `doors`, `lift`,
  `map_objects`, `level_triggers`, `countdown_timer`, `command_sequencer`
- **Rendering:** `model_draw`, `object_render`
- **Front end:** `frontend`, `pause_menu`, `hud`, `save_password`, `memcard`
- **Audio:** `audio`, `audio_control`, `music_control`
- A few units (`game_20000_*`, `game_helpers7`) still hold functions whose subsystem is not
  settled yet.

Unit file names describe what the code does. They are not evidence of the original file
layout. Shared types live in `include/`, one owning header per subsystem (`ACTOR.H`,
`LEVEL.H`, `TASK.H`, ...).

The code follows id Software's Quake III C style: `Prefix_VerbNoun` functions with a module
prefix (`Actor_PlayAnimation`, `Door_Init`), `lowerCamel_t` types, `lowerCamel` members, `g_`
globals, K&R layout with spaces inside parentheses (`.clang-format`), and a box banner above
each function. Names that come from evidence outside this game keep their original spelling:
Sony library names, and names from lineage source. Probe's later *Forsaken* (PC) shares
framework code with this game, and its `Tasker.c` is the direct descendant of `src/tasker.c`
(`TaskerInit`, `TASK`).

Names are semantic wherever there is evidence for them; 7 functions are still named after
their address (`f_xxxxx`), each with a note saying what was checked. Comments in the source
mark where each name comes from (`name: inferred from ...`, `names invented`).

The renderer at `0x80048f54`–`0x800588bb` is hand-written MIPS/GTE assembly in the original.
It lives in `asm/` as heavily annotated `.s` files assembled by ASPSX, and is counted
separately from C.

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `src/` | Reconstructed C units. Every function here is a full byte match. |
| `include/` | Shared types and declarations, one owner per type or symbol (`include/README.TXT`). |
| `asm/` | The 11 hand-written renderer units. |
| `asm/lib/` | 29 Sony library modules that match no archived SDK version, as annotated assembly (`docs/notes/library_asm.md`). |
| `config/` | Per-unit symbol maps (function and data addresses and sizes, every referenced symbol), `data.json` (initialized data placement), BSS and section layout, the gate's hash contract, the toolchain lock. |
| `tools/` | Build, verify, gate, diff and report tools (Python, standard library only except `diff.py`). |
| `analysis/` | Sony library identification (`runtime_*.py`), the link plan, startup and GP layout, symbol inventory, validation scripts. |
| `reports/` | Generated results: `latest.json` (per-function verification), `progress.json`, `link_plan.json` (the remaining gaps). |
| `docs/notes/` | Notes on the toolchain, GCC 2.5.7 codegen, the task system, the heap and the linker. |
| `AGENTS.md` | Working rules for contributors, human or automated. |

## How verification works

- **`tools/build.py`** compiles one unit with the original DOS toolchain under DOSBox-X.
- **`tools/verify.py`** builds every unit and compares each function and data item with the
  retail bytes. The comparison includes the target of every relocation, so a function that calls
  the wrong function or names the wrong global does not count as matched.
- **`tools/gate.py`** is the final check:
  1. It rebuilds everything into a fresh directory.
  2. Its own linker applies every relocation and places the matched code and data over the
     original executable.
  3. It requires the whole PS-X EXE to hash to the retail SHA-256.
  4. It writes a per-byte provenance record and checks it against `verify.py`.

  The only success output is a single `GATE OK` line. On failure it names the unit and function
  behind every differing byte.

Only code that passes all of this is in `src/`. Partial reconstructions are kept out of the
build.

## Requirements

You need to supply:

- your own copy of the retail executable, at
  `../games/Alien Trilogy (PS1 USA)/extracted/SLUS_000.07`;
- the PsyQ toolchain under `../toolchain/`, with the exact files whose hashes are pinned in
  `config/toolchain.lock.json` (GCC 2.5.7 `C257`, the ASPSX assemblers, and
  `binutils-mips-decompals` v0.10);
- the Runtime Library 3.3 SDK under `../sdk/`, and `../shared-tools/psyqobj.py`;
- Python 3 and [DOSBox-X](https://dosbox-x.com/) at `C:\DOSBox-X\dosbox-x.exe`;
- `capstone` (`pip install -r requirements.txt`), needed only by `tools/diff.py`.

Paths are relative to this checkout, so it must sit next to those directories.

## Usage

```
python tools/gate.py                       # whole-executable byte gate (about 2 minutes)
python tools/verify.py                     # per-function verification, writes reports/latest.json
python tools/verify.py --units player --output builds/player.json   # one unit
python tools/build.py --source src/player.c                         # compile one unit
python tools/diff.py --object builds/job-*/INPUT.OBJ --symbol-map config/player.json --function <name>
python tools/rules.py --report-only        # code-rule check: matched under the rules, MATCH-PENDING
python tools/reports.py --jobs 6           # gate, verify, library reports, rules, link plan, PROGRESS.md
```

Run the gate from a clean tree; it refuses to bank anything else. Tool tests use
`python -m unittest tools/test_<tool>.py`. `tools/test_elf_lnk.py` needs two ELF fixtures
that are not published.

If you are an agent tasked with modifying this repository or any derivative project, please ensure you read the documentation in /docs, including PORTING.md.

## Open issues

- **Remaining gaps:** the 452 gaps listed in `reports/link_plan.json`.
- **MATCH-PENDING functions:** 8 byte-exact functions whose honest spelling is still unknown,
  listed in `config/match_pending.json` with what was tried (`Menu_CreditsLineTask`,
  `Menu_MessageBoxType`, `Card_WriteFile`, `Particle_DrawDebris`, `Object_PickupsTask`,
  `Door_Blocked`, `Door_PrepareModels`, `Lift_PrepareModels`).
- **`_spu_RXX`:** Sony's `S_GKS` and `S_SCA` modules imply two different addresses for it, so
  both are rebuilt as library assembly instead of being certified as Runtime 3.3.
- **Layout:** the gate places matched code and data at the addresses in the symbol maps. A link
  from source alone, without the original as fallback, is not attempted yet.
- **Names and types:** a byte match proves the generated code, not the names or types. Some
  names and struct layouts are still provisional.

## Contributing

Read `AGENTS.md` first. In short:

- only full matches enter `src/`;
- no inline assembly outside the permitted renderer and library ranges;
- no magic numbers;
- no fake code or padding to move a score;
- Quake III naming and layout (`config/style_renames.json`, `.clang-format`);
- nothing is "matched" until the gate prints `GATE OK`, and a function counts as finished only
  when `tools/rules.py` also passes it.

## Legal

The reconstructed source, tools and documentation are released under the MIT License
(`LICENSE`). *Alien Trilogy* and its data belong to their respective owners. PlayStation, PsyQ and
the Runtime Library belong to Sony Interactive Entertainment and SN Systems. None of them is
included here, and you need your own legally obtained copy of the game to build anything.

# EGA Trek port

A native port of *EGA Trek* (1988, v1.0, Nels Anderson) for **macOS (Apple Silicon)** and modern web browsers via **WebAssembly**.

The port statically decompiles and recompiles the original 16-bit real-mode MS-DOS binary (`TREK.EXE`, Turbo Pascal 4.0) into portable C++20, running inside a lightweight PC environment that emulates the 1 MB real-mode address space, EGA planar graphics, PC speaker audio, PIT timer, and DOS/BIOS interrupts.

This repository contains **only clean-room engine code, tools, and build infrastructure**. No copyrighted game files or derived generated code are committed to the repository. The recompiler processes your legally owned copy of `TREK.EXE` at build time.

> [!NOTE]
> **Disclaimer**: *Star Trek* is a registered trademark of Paramount Global / CBS Studios. This project is an independent, non-commercial educational and digital preservation research project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Paramount, CBS, or Nels Anderson. No copyrighted game binaries, media assets, or decompiled code are distributed in this repository.

---

## Architecture & Design

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                          Host Presentation Layer                       |
|   macOS Native: SDL3 + Metal/Cocoa    |    Web: SDL3 + WebGL + IDBFS   |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                             engine (C++20)                             |
|                                                                        |
|  +--------------------+  +--------------------+  +------------------+  |
|  |    dos::Machine    |  |     dos::Ega       |  |   dos::Speaker   |  |
|  | 1 MB real-mode mem |  | 640x350 planar mem |  | PIT ch2 square-  |  |
|  | Register file & CFG|  | 16-color palette   |  | wave audio synth |  |
|  | Fast block dispatch|  | 4:3 letterboxing   |  | Cooperative yield|  |
|  +--------------------+  +--------------------+  +------------------+  |
|            |                                                           |
|  +--------------------+  +--------------------+                        |
|  | recompiled segments|  |    Interpreter     |                        |
|  | (16 C++ switch-    |  |  fallback for self-|                        |
|  |  dispatched units) |  |  modifying code    |                        |
|  +--------------------+  +--------------------+                        |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    ^
                                    | static translation
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                        tools/trekre (Python 3.12)                      |
|   8086 decoder  *  CFG discovery  *  no-return & relocation hints       |
+------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    ^
                                    | binary analysis
                            Original TREK.EXE
```

### Static Recompiler (`tools/trekre`)
The recompiler parses the 16-bit MZ executable, resolves relocations, recovers Turbo Pascal 4 runtime units, and performs iterative control-flow discovery. It handles:
- **Relocated code segments**: Recognizes Borland `Graph` driver and font memory copies and relocates references accordingly.
- **No-return runtime procedures**: Avoids decoding invalid dead paths following `Halt` or runtime error handlers.
- **Segment translation**: Emits C++ switch-dispatched blocks (`build/generated/seg_XXXX.cpp`) compiled as a static library.

### Emulation Layer (`engine/src/dos`)
- **`trek::dos::Machine`**: Manages the 1 MB real-mode memory map, CPU register state, flags, segment registers, and BIOS/DOS interrupts (`INT 10h`, `INT 16h`, `INT 1Ah`, `INT 21h`).
- **Dynamic & Self-Modifying Code Fallback**: An integrated 8086 interpreter seamlessly handles self-modifying instructions (e.g. Borland runtime self-patching at `0x0AAB:0x0010` and `0x1521:0x0099`).
- **EGA Display (`dos::Ega`)**: Emulates the 640×350 16-color EGA planar layout, CRT controller registers, and text-mode blink counter. Preserves authentic CRT 4:3 proportions via SDL logical presentation letterboxing.
- **Audio & PIT Timing (`dos::Speaker`)**: Synthesizes 44.1 kHz square-wave audio from 8253 PIT channel 2. Cooperative `Crt.Delay` yielding gives authentic sound duration and synchronized visual effects across presentation frames while maintaining smooth 60 FPS presentation.

---

## Prerequisites & Environment Setup

The repository uses [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/) for pinned development environments and [Docker](https://www.docker.com/) for containerized builds.

### 1. Install mise Tools
```zsh
mise trust
mise install
```
This provisions Python 3.12, `uv`, CMake, and Ninja.

### 2. Container Engine
Docker (or Colima on macOS Apple Silicon) is required for containerized Linux CI runs and WebAssembly compilation:
```zsh
# If using Colima on Apple Silicon:
colima start --cpu 4 --memory 8
```

---

## Usage Guide

### 1. Game Binary Setup
Place your original `TREK.EXE` (along with `TREK.DOC` and `TREK.REF`) in the directory directly above this repository:
```
EGATREK10/
  ├── TREK.EXE
  ├── TREK.DOC
  ├── TREK.REF
  └── egatrek-port/      <-- this repository
```
*(You can also set the `TREK_DATA` environment variable to point to any directory containing `TREK.EXE`.)*

### 2. Static Recompilation
Generate the portable C++ code from `TREK.EXE`:
```zsh
./scripts/recomp.zsh
```
This analyzes the binary and writes the generated translation units to `build/generated/`.

### 3. Native macOS Build & Run
Build the native Apple Silicon app:
```zsh
./scripts/build.zsh
```
Run the game natively:
```zsh
./scripts/run.zsh
```

### 4. macOS Application Bundle Packaging
Package a standalone, codesigned macOS application bundle (`EGA Trek.app`) with custom Tahoe squircle icon:
```zsh
./scripts/bundle.zsh
```
Output:
- `dist/EGA Trek.app`
- `dist/EGA Trek.zip`

To notarize and staple the bundle for distribution (requires Apple Developer credentials):
```zsh
./scripts/notarize.zsh
```

### 5. WebAssembly Browser Build
Build the WebAssembly version in the Emscripten container and serve it locally:
```zsh
./scripts/build-wasm.zsh --serve
```
Open `http://localhost:8080/egatrek.html` in any modern web browser.
- **Responsive Viewport**: Letterboxed 4:3 presentation that automatically adapts to any window resolution or Retina display without edge clipping.
- **Persistent Saves**: Saves written in-game are persisted in the browser via IndexedDB (`IDBFS`).

---

## In-Game Controls & Features

| Key / Command | Action |
|---|---|
| **Arrow Keys / Keypad** | Navigate ship and menus |
| **Space / Enter** | Advance text, accept command |
| **Shift-F1** | **Boss Key**: Instantly flips to a fake DOS prompt screen (`dir/w`) |
| **`SAVE`** | Save current game state to `TREK.SAV` (persisted in macOS Application Support or browser IndexedDB) |
| **`RESTORE`** | Restore saved game |
| **`Q` / Cmd-Q** | Quit game |

---

## Development Guide

### Repository Layout

```
engine/                  C++20 game engine and platform shell
  ├── CMakeLists.txt     Build configuration for native and Emscripten targets
  ├── resources/         macOS Info.plist and AppIcon.icns
  ├── src/
  │   ├── app/           Application shell (main.cpp, host key mapping)
  │   ├── core/          Byte reading, MZ image parsing, asset path resolution
  │   ├── dos/           PC machine, 8086 interpreter, EGA, PIT speaker, ROM font
  │   └── gfx/           EGA surface and Borland BGI stroke font renderer
  ├── web/               HTML/CSS shell page for WebAssembly build
  └── tests/             C++ unit tests (doctest), lockstep, and headless test runners
tools/
  ├── trekre/            Python 3.12 reverse-engineering & recompiler toolsuite
  │   └── trekre/        Decoder, CFG generator, C++ code emitter, BGI decoders
  └── ghidra/            Headless Ghidra analysis scripts (PyGhidra)
docker/
  ├── ci.Dockerfile      Linux CI environment (Clang, SDL3, Unicorn, doctest)
  ├── wasm.Dockerfile    Emscripten WebAssembly build environment
  └── analysis.Dockerfile Ghidra 12 analysis container for Apple Silicon
scripts/                 macOS zsh build, test, and lifecycle scripts
docs/
  └── findings.md        Technical analysis of original 1988 binary structure
```

### Running Tests

#### 1. Native macOS Test Suite
Runs all 27 Python recompiler tests and all 5 C++ test suites on macOS:
```zsh
./scripts/test.zsh
```

Test suites include:
- `unit`: Core byte reader, MZ loader, font rendering, and machine execution tests.
- `instruction_corpus`: Compares instruction decoder and flag calculation against the Unicorn x86 emulator across 7,500+ cases.
- `game_headless`: Multi-thousand-frame gameplay session exercising navigation, weapons, computer commands, boss screen, and game saving.
- `game_lockstep`: Runs recompiled code and interpreted code in lockstep block by block, verifying state parity.
- `app_smoke`: Verification of SDL application startup, frame ticking, and exit.

#### 2. Linux Container CI Test Suite
Tests run inside the containerized Linux environment matching GitHub Actions CI:
```zsh
./scripts/test.zsh --docker
```

#### 3. WebAssembly Node.js Test Suite
Builds the WebAssembly binaries and runs the test suite under Node.js:
```zsh
./scripts/build-wasm.zsh
```

### Reverse Engineering & Analysis Tools

- **Binary Inventory**: Dumps segment maps, extracted strings, and BGI driver/font assets into `out/`:
  ```zsh
  ./scripts/inventory.zsh
  ```
- **Headless Ghidra Analysis**: Runs automated Ghidra decompilation inside the Docker analysis container:
  ```zsh
  ./scripts/analyze.zsh
  ```
- **Generate App Icon**: Regenerates the continuous superellipse Tahoe squircle icon:
  ```zsh
  python3 scripts/generate_icon.py
  ```

---

## Clean-Room & Security Policy

- Original binary files (`*.EXE`, `*.DOC`, `*.REF`, `*.SAV`, `*.CHR`, `*.BGI`) are ignored by git and never committed.
- Recompiled C++ translation units (`build/generated/*.cpp`) are generated locally from the user's binary and never committed.
- All test suites use mock byte sequences or synthetic MZ executables to enable verification in clean CI environments without external game assets.
