# Monopoly (1985): reconstructed source and browser port

This repository contains a 1985 freeware Monopoly game for MS-DOS (IBM PC with CGA). The game is credited to Don Phillip Gibson (MS-DOS adaptation, version 5.1) and was distributed as freeware by John Capers. The included `MONOFREE.TXT` invites anyone to "distribute, copy, or decompile and change" it.

The repository holds three things built from the game:

1. **The reconstructed Turbo Pascal source** (`src/`). It was decompiled from the original binaries and is proven to compile back to them byte for byte.
2. **A browser port** (`web/`). The reconstructed source is compiled to JavaScript and runs on an emulation of the PC and of the original Turbo Pascal runtime. It reproduces the original screen for screen and plays the same sounds.
3. **The tools and tests** that prove both of the above.

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `src/` | `MONOPOLY.PAS` (loader), `MONOCODE.PAS` + `MONOCOD1.INC` + `MONOCOD2.INC` (game and overlays) |
| `original/` | The original freeware files: `monopoly.com`, `MONOCODE.CHN`, `MONOCODE.000`, `MONOGRAF.GRA`, `MONOFREE.TXT` |
| `docs/SOURCE.md` | Guide to the source: structure, data model, turn flow, every procedure |
| `docs/DECOMPILATION.md` | How the source was recovered and how it is verified |
| `docs/WEBPORT.md` | How the browser port works and how it was verified, including sound |
| `verify/` | Rebuild the originals from `src/` and compare (`verify.sh`) |
| `web/` | The browser port, its Pascal-to-JavaScript compiler (`web/tools/pas2js.py`) and its tests |

## Play it in a browser

    cd web && python3 -m http.server 8000      # then open http://localhost:8000/

Click the screen to start; sound needs a user action in the browser. During the dice roll, F1 toggles sound and F2 saves the game; on the "Who are the players?" screen, F2 loads a saved game. Saved games are kept in the browser's localStorage. On phones and tablets an on-screen PC keyboard appears below the screen (the "Keyboard" button shows or hides it).

**Speed.** The "Speed" control below the screen sets how fast the sound effects that depended on the PC's speed run (token steps, sirens, house sweeps, cash counters): **Fast PC (DOSBox)**, the default, as on the faster PCs of the early 1990s and DOSBox's default setting, or **IBM PC 4.77 MHz**, the machine the game was written for (see `docs/WEBPORT.md`).

**Online play.** After the click, a menu in the game's own style offers **L** (play on this computer, the original game), **C** (create an online game), **J** (join one) or **S** (sound test: every sound of the game, one letter each, Esc to go back).
- **Creating a game:** the creator, the host, gets a four-letter game code to give to the others, up to four players in all, and starts the game when everyone has joined. **S** starts a new game and **F2** starts the original "load a saved game" screen.
- **Taking turns:** every player sees the game exactly as in the original. Only the player whose turn it is can type or tap; anyone else's keys are ignored.
- **Talking:** a chat line under the screen is there for what the game expects players to say aloud, such as auction bids and trade prices.
- **Reloads and absences:** a player who reloads rejoins with the same code and name. If a player is gone for 20 seconds on their turn, the host can play for them.
- **Requirements:** online play needs `web/api.php` on a PHP 8 server (see `docs/WEBPORT.md`).

**Display and font.** The port can show the screen as a VGA (the default) or a CGA would.
- **VGA:** text screens use an 8×16 font in 9×16 character cells at 720×400; the board stays in 320×200 CGA graphics, as on a VGA PC.
- **CGA:** everything uses the 8×8 font, as on the game's original 1985 target.

The real IBM fonts are not included; the port has its own. To get the original look, run `web/tools/extract_pcfont.sh` once. It takes the 8×8 and VGA 8×16 fonts from the BIOS of your own DOSBox and writes `web/pcfont.bin` and `web/pcfont16.bin`, which the port then uses automatically. Without both files, you can also load any 2048-byte (8×8) or 4096-byte (8×16) font file with the control below the screen; when both are present, they are always used and that control is hidden.

## Build the original programs from the source

You need Turbo Pascal 3 and Borland's `GRAPH.P` and `GRAPH.BIN`, which are not included.

1. **Compile the game:**
   - Work file `monocode`, typed in lower case. The overlay file name `monocode.000` is stored inside the `.CHN` exactly as typed.
   - Compiler options → **cHn-file**.
   - Output: `MONOCODE.CHN` and `MONOCODE.000`.
2. **Compile the loader:**
   - Work file `MONOPOLY`.
   - Compiler options → **Com-file**, minimum cOde segment size `0C72`, minimum Data segment size `05CE`.
   - Output: `MONOPOLY.COM`.

`verify/verify.sh` does all of this headless and checks the result:
- It compiles both programs with Turbo Pascal 3.02 under the emu2 DOS emulator.
- It relocates the output onto the 1985 runtime the originals were built with, which differs slightly from the 3.02 runtime.
- It compares the result with `original/` using `cmp`.

The result: `MONOCODE.CHN`, `MONOCODE.000` and `MONOPOLY.COM` are all byte-identical to the originals.

## Notes

- **Names.** Compiled code keeps no identifiers or comments, so all names in `src/` were chosen during the reconstruction. Each procedure and global carries its original address in a comment.
- **Not included:** Borland's Turbo Pascal compiler and `GRAPH.P`/`GRAPH.BIN`, and IBM's PC font.
- **Trademark.** Monopoly is a trademark of its owner; the game's title screen carries the original 1985 notice.

octplane-printmaster-web-readme-md.text:
# PrintMaster, rebuilt

PrintMaster, the Unison World greeting-card program of 1985, read off a 1987
Atari ST floppy and put back together in a browser.

The disk is an ordinary 360 KB single-sided FAT12 volume, so getting the files
out is easy. The work was in the formats and the layout rules: what a shape
record looks like, how borders tile, where the page geometry table lives, how a
line of text advances. Those came from disassembling `PM.TOS`, not from
guessing at screenshots.

## The site

Three pages, each a self-contained HTML file with the fonts and clip art
embedded as base64:

| page              | what it is                                                      |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `card.html`       | Greeting card: front and inside panels, borders, artwork slots   |
| `letterhead.html` | Stationery: top and bottom bands on a full sheet                 |
| `editor.html`     | Graphic Editor: the 88 x 52 bitmap editor and its command set    |

`src/` holds them exactly as published as Claude Artifacts, byte for byte, so
they can be pushed back there unchanged. `site/` is the built copy, which adds a
link between the pages and `local-runtime.js` — a small stand-in for the artifact
host so that saving and file export work on a plain static server. Saved designs
go to `localStorage`, so they stay in one browser on one machine.

```
python3 build.py        # src/ -> site/, no dependencies
```

## What was recovered

Everything visual on the disk uses **one record type**: a byte of bytes-per-row,
a byte of rows, a big-endian width, then 1 bpp rows with MSB leftmost. Clip art,
borders, menu illustrations and the tiling icons are all that same container at
different strides.

| | |
|---|---|
| Clip art | 122 shapes, 88 x 52, 578 B each (`SLIB.SHP`) |
| Borders | 11 sets of corners and edges |
| Fonts | 9, with real cell heights and advance widths from `FONTS1.FSZ` |
| Printer drivers | 17 `.PRG` child processes, six-entry ABI recovered |
| Dot pitch | 120 dpi across, 72 down — aspect 3:5 |
| `PM.TOS` | 17,149 instructions, 28 OS entry points, no GEM AES/VDI at all |

Page geometry is a word table at `0x13a64` indexed by page type; artwork repeat
counts are at `0x14160`; lines advance by `height * size + 4`.

- [`docs/FORMATS.md`](docs/FORMATS.md) — the file formats
- [`docs/REVERSING.md`](docs/REVERSING.md) — the disassembly notes and the driver ABI

## Tools

Python 3, no dependencies except where noted.

```
tools/pm_extract.py  Printmaster.MFM.img assets/   # FAT12 reader, every asset to PNG + manifest
tools/pm_doc.py      assets/docs/                  # .SIG .BAN .LET .CAR .CAL documents to JSON
tools/pm_render.py   DOORS.SIG out.png             # render a document using the recovered layout rules
tools/pm_disasm.py   PM.TOS                        # 68000 segment map, syscalls, function map (needs capstone)
```

`pm_doc.py` and `pm_render.py` import `pm_extract`, so run them from `tools/` or
put it on the path.

## Provenance and rights

**Original owner.** PrintMaster was published in March 1985 by **Unison World,
Inc.**, 2150 Shattuck Avenue, Berkeley, California. No individual author is
credited on the disk or in the catalogue records, and `PM.TOS` carries no
copyright string at all — the title screen is drawn with the bitmap font, so
there is nothing in the binary for `strings` to find.

**This disk is a 1987 build**, not the 1985 original. Its own sample documents
date it: `HOTEL.LET` references 1986 and `RMS1.CAL` references 1987.

**Where the rights went.** Unison World was acquired by Kyocera, which shipped
the product as Kyocera Unison through PrintMaster Plus 2.0 in September 1988.
The brand then passed to MicroLogic Software (PrintMaster Gold, 1993),
Mindscape (1995), The Learning Company (1998), Mattel, Gores, and Riverdeep,
which took all of Brøderbund in August 2002. PrintMaster is still sold today
under the Broderbund brand, published by Encore under licence from the
Riverdeep / Houghton Mifflin Harcourt lineage; Encore's assets were bought by
Sereno Ventures, LLC in November 2017.

That chain tracks the *brand and product line*. Whether copyright in this 1987
codebase travelled with it is not something the public record settles, and no
registration has been confirmed against the US Copyright Office register.

**PrintMaster's own interface was found infringing.** In *Broderbund Software,
Inc. v. Unison World, Inc.*, 648 F. Supp. 1127 (N.D. Cal. 1986), the court held
that PrintMaster's menu screens copied the structure, sequence and "total
concept and feel" of Brøderbund's The Print Shop. It is a landmark look-and-feel
decision. The Print Shop copyright was held by **Pixellite Software** — David
Balsam and Martin Kahn — with Brøderbund as exclusive licensee, so the interface
Unison World shipped was not theirs to have copied. The case concerned the IBM
PC version and the program was afterwards reworked to a different look and feel;
whether this ST build is before or after that rework is unresolved here.

**What that means for this repo.** The disk image, `PM.TOS` and the 17 `.PRG`
drivers are the program itself and are left out — `.gitignore` covers them. Drop
the image next to the tools to re-run the extraction yourself. `assets/` does
hold the decoded art and fonts, and the pages embed them; that is derivative of
a work which has never been placed in the public domain and whose commercial
successors are still trading. Treat all of it as preservation and study
material.

## Licence

The code here — the tools, the build script, the shim, the pages — is MIT, see
[`LICENSE`](LICENSE). That covers none of the 1985–87 material described above.

# WC1 Reflight ![Confed fighters and a Kilrathi fighter under fire in the chase view, rendered at 1920x1080](docs/images/space-combat.png) *Wing Commander* (Origin Systems, 1990) for today's computers: a native, cross-platform reimplementation in C# / .NET 10 that plays the original DOS game data, with a modern Vulkan renderer, sharp ships and text at any screen resolution, and the original music and gameplay. > **No game data is included.** You need your own copy of Wing Commander, for example the GOG > release "Wing Commander 1+2". *Wing Commander* is a trademark of Electronic Arts; this is an > unofficial fan project. ## What is new compared to the original game | Area | Original (DOS, 1990) | WC1 Reflight | | --- | --- | --- | | Platform | DOS (today: DOSBox or the Kilrathi Saga build) | Native Windows, Linux and macOS; one NativeAOT executable, no emulator | | Rendering | 320x200, 256 colours | Vulkan renderer (MoltenVK on macOS) with SDL fallback; resizable window, fullscreen, 4:3 aspect correction or square pixels, nearest / sharp-bilinear / linear filtering, integer scaling, vsync | | Ships in space | Pixel sprites scaled inside 320x200 | Ships, missiles, explosions and asteroids are drawn at your screen resolution (smooth scaling and rotation, far sharper ship models); the cockpit and HUD stay pixel-exact on top | | Motion | The space view moves in steps, at most 20 per second | Ships, shots, stars and the target brackets glide at your display's refresh rate (60, 144 Hz ...), between the game's 20 simulation steps per second | | Text | Four pixel fonts | All text drawn at screen resolution: crisp vectorized originals or modern replacement fonts (see [Fonts](#fonts)); text drawn into off-screen buffers (space view, scenes, saved backgrounds) is followed too | | Help | Printed manual | **F10** shows the flight controls next to the cockpit (in the side margins of widescreen displays, otherwise as a panel) | | Menus | None | **Esc** opens a pause menu (in flight, in the rooms and on the title) with **settings**: volumes, fullscreen, filter, aspect ratio, vsync, sharp text, fonts, key help and **flight keys** (every flight control can be put on another key); saved in `config.json` | | Briefing | The wall screen shows the same shrunken, unreadable map in every briefing | The wall screen shows this mission's nav map, its text sharp and readable | | Mouse | The cursor moves with the game's 16 frames per second | The cursor follows the mouse at the display's refresh rate | | Sound | AdLib / Sound Blaster | The original Origin FX music and sound effects on an emulated OPL2 (port of ymfm) | | Saves | Next to the game | In your user data folder; existing DOS saves are imported automatically | | Controls | DOS keyboard repeat | Key repeat identical on every system, Alt+X quits anywhere | | Fixes | | Planets drawn as sprites, cockpit display static and cockpit explosion animation restored (`--ks-literal` returns to the Kilrathi Saga look) | Gameplay, simulation, AI and timing follow the reverse-engineered Kilrathi Saga build ([neuromancer/wc1-re](https://github.com/neuromancer/wc1-re)), running on a deterministic virtual clock: the same input gives the same mission, which also makes the whole game testable. ### Side by side The same moment, rendered at 1440x1080 by the original 320x200 path and by WC1 Reflight. Ships, shots and explosions keep their detail instead of being shrunk into 320x200 first: ![Ships: the original 320x200 picture scaled up next to WC1 Reflight](docs/images/compare-ships.png) Text is drawn at screen resolution, here in the replacement font of conversations and briefings: ![Subtitle text: the original pixel font scaled up next to the sharp replacement font](docs/images/compare-text.png) The briefing's wall screen shows the mission's own map, its text readable: ![Briefing board: the fixed, unreadable art of the original next to this mission's map in WC1 Reflight](docs/images/compare-board.png) ### In the game ![Cockpit in flight: sharp cockpit displays and radio message, the flight controls (F10) in the side margins of a 16:9 screen](docs/images/cockpit-key-help.png) *Cockpit at 1920x1080: radio messages and cockpit displays at screen resolution, the key help (F10) in the side margins.*
Esc opens the pause menu in flight, in the rooms and on the title. Settings apply at once and are saved in config.json.
Conversations and briefings in Tektur. The kill board in the CHAWP chalk font.
Flight keys: every control on the key you want. The briefing board with the mission's map.
The screenshots are rendered by [`scripts/readme-screenshots.py`](scripts/readme-screenshots.py) from a scripted, headless run of the game (`wc1tool snap --gpu`). They show game art, which is copyright Electronic Arts. ## Getting started 1. Install the [.NET 10 SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download). 2. Copy `config.example.json` to `config.json` and set `gameDirectory` to your Wing Commander folder (the install folder or its `GAMEDAT` folder). `config.json` stays on your machine. 3. Run the game: ```bash dotnet run --project src/WingCommander -c Release ``` The game directory can also be given with `--game ` or the `WC1_GAME_DIR` environment variable. Useful options: | Option | Effect | | --- | --- | | `--fullscreen`, `--window`, `--scale N` | Fullscreen or window (overrides the setting); window size N times 320x240 | | `--filter nearest\|sharp\|linear`, `--square-pixels`, `--integer`, `--no-vsync` | Picture options | | `--renderer auto\|vulkan\|sdl` | Renderer (default: Vulkan with SDL fallback) | | `--classic-space` | Draw space objects into the 320x200 picture like the original | | `--classic-text`, `--original-fonts` | Original pixel text, or vectorized original fonts instead of the replacement fonts | | `--ks-literal` | Kilrathi Saga look (no visual fixes) | | `--skip-intro`, `--no-audio` | Start faster, play silently | | `-- ` | The original game's command-line switches | In flight, all original controls apply; **Esc** opens the pause menu with the settings, **F10** toggles the key help, **Alt+X** quits. Settings > Flight keys puts any flight control on another key (the key help shows your keys). The settings are saved in `config.json`; command-line options override them for one run. ### Native executable On Windows, `build.bat` builds a native, self-contained and trimmed executable (NativeAOT) into `publish\win-x64` (`build.bat win-arm64` for ARM): just `wc1.exe` (about 4 MB, fonts compiled in), `SDL3.dll` and `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`. It needs Visual Studio or the Build Tools with the "Desktop development with C++" workload. On Linux and macOS: ```bash dotnet publish src/WingCommander -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:DebugType=none -o publish/linux-x64 # or osx-arm64 ``` Put `config.json` next to the executable (or in a parent folder). See [docs/BUILD.md](docs/BUILD.md). ## Fonts With the Vulkan renderer the game's text is drawn at output resolution: the four game fonts are replaced by these fonts (sources and licences in [`assets/fonts/`](assets/fonts/), compiled into the game): | Game font | Used for | Replacement | | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | conversations, briefings, prompts, room labels | **Tektur** SemiBold by Adam Jagosz, copyright 2023 The Tektur Project Authors ([github.com/hyvyys/Tektur](https://github.com/hyvyys/Tektur), [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Tektur)), licensed under the [SIL Open Font License 1.1](https://openfontlicense.org) | | 1 and 2 | HUD messages, cockpit displays, speed readouts, nav map, training simulator | **SPACE WING LEADER** by SFO, made with [FontStruct](https://fontstruct.com/fontstructions/show/2704307), licensed under [CC BY 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0/) | | 3 | chalk board (kill board) in the rec room | **CHAWP**, copyright (c) 2013 Ancient Wisdom Productions ([awpny.com](http://www.awpny.com)), Reserved Font Name CHAWP, licensed under the [SIL Open Font License 1.1](https://openfontlicense.org) | ![The kill board: original chalk font next to CHAWP](docs/images/compare-kill-board.png) The replacement glyphs are fitted into the original glyph cells, so the game's text layout is unchanged; characters a font does not have and the gauge symbols of font 2 keep the original design, vectorized. The classic 320x200 picture (SDL renderer, `--classic-text`) always shows the original fonts; `--original-fonts` keeps the vectorized originals at output resolution. ## Project layout ``` src/WingCommander.Core data formats, fixed-point math, virtual clock, rendering contracts src/WingCommander.Graphics 320x200 raster library: shapes, fonts, palettes, text tracking src/WingCommander.Audio OPL2 emulation, Origin FX music and sound effects src/WingCommander.Simulation space flight: objects, weapons, collisions, AI, missions src/WingCommander.Game game flow, campaign, rooms, briefings, cutscenes src/WingCommander.Game.Flight cockpit, HUD, flight controls and sequences src/WingCommander.Render.Vulkan Vulkan renderer (classic layer, sprites, text, overlay) src/WingCommander.Host.Sdl SDL3 window, input, audio, fallback renderer src/WingCommander the game executable (wc1) src/WingCommander.Tools wc1tool: data inspection, exports, headless screenshots tests/ xunit tests per project (game-data tests run when config.json is set) docs/ architecture, decisions, analysis of the original, progress docs/images/ README screenshots (scripts/readme-screenshots.py) ``` Start with [docs/README.md](docs/README.md) for the architecture, the analysis of the original code and the porting notes. ## Roadmap - Backgrounds widened to 16:9 and 16:10 for the rooms and scenes - Joystick and gamepad support - 3D ship models (glTF, PBR) and ray-traced effects on capable GPUs ## License WC1 Reflight is free software under the [GNU General Public License v3.0](LICENSE). It is a translation of the reconstructed source of [neuromancer/wc1-re](https://github.com/neuromancer/wc1-re), which is GPL-3.0 as well. Bundled third-party components keep their own licences, all GPL-compatible and reproduced in [`THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`](THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt): ymfm (BSD-3-Clause), Tektur and CHAWP (SIL Open Font License 1.1), SPACE WING LEADER (CC BY 3.0); SDL3 (zlib) and Vortice.Vulkan (MIT) come as NuGet packages. *Wing Commander* and its game data are copyright Electronic Arts. They are not part of this project and not covered by its licence. ## Credits - [neuromancer/wc1-re](https://github.com/neuromancer/wc1-re): the reverse-engineered C source of the Kilrathi Saga build that this reimplementation follows. - [ymfm](https://github.com/aaronsgiles/ymfm) by Aaron Giles (BSD-3-Clause): the OPL2 emulator ported to C#. - All third-party licences ship with the executable in `THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt`. - [SDL3](https://www.libsdl.org/) via [ppy.SDL3-CS](https://github.com/ppy/SDL3-CS) and [Vortice.Vulkan](https://github.com/amerkoleci/Vortice.Vulkan). - The fonts listed above.

# POLE CHUDES (1992–1993) — reverse-engineered source code

**Reverse-engineered reconstruction of the original DOS game «Поле чудес» by Vadim Bashurov (Arzamas-16, 1992–1993).**

The source code was recovered by reverse engineering the original `POLE.EXE`. The reconstruction preserves the original program structure, procedures, variables, algorithms and formulas, and is written in **Turbo Pascal 7.0** for MS-DOS.

The original program was written for DOS. This reconstruction works in DOS or in an emulator. It uses VGA mode `10h` (640×350×16), direct access to video memory at `$A000`, and does **not** use Crt, Graph or BGI units.

---

## Legal notice

This repository contains a reverse-engineered reconstruction of the original 1992–1993 DOS game «Поле чудес».

- **Original game**: © 1992–1993 Vadim Bashurov, Arzamas-16, USSR/Russia
- **Turbo Pascal runtime library**: © Borland International

I publish this reconstruction strictly for historical, educational and archival purposes.

This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by the copyright holders of the television game show «Поле чудес» or any related rights holders.

If you represent the rights holders and want me to take this repository down, open an issue or contact me.

---

## Requirements

The game runs **only under MS-DOS** (or a DOS emulator such as DOSBox). This is not a port to a modern operating system.

The reconstructed code retains direct interaction with IBM PC hardware:

- VGA mode `$10` (640×350×16);
- direct access to video memory at `$A000`;
- BIOS `INT 10h` services;
- keyboard via BIOS `INT 16h`;
- mouse support via `INT 33h`;
- PC speaker sound via ports `$42` / `$61`;
- the data files `POLE.LIB`, `POLE.FNT`, `POLE.OVL` and `POLE.PIC` placed next to the executable.

## Building and running

### DOSBox + Turbo Pascal 7

Install DOSBox (or DOSBox-X / DOSBox Staging) and Turbo Pascal 7.0, then compile the reconstructed source. Place `POLE.LIB`, `POLE.FNT`, `POLE.OVL` and `POLE.PIC` in the same directory as the resulting `EXE`.

elthial-crescent-hawks-inception-sdl-por.text:
A readable C17 reconstruction of the 1988 DOS game.

This repository is a C17 reconstruction of the 1988 DOS game. Its purpose is preservation: represent the executable's procedures, data, control flow and BattleTech rules as readable C while retaining a direct route back to the assembly evidence. This repository starts at the consolidated v1.0 preservation snapshot. The monorepo's development commit history is intentionally not imported. This is not a redesign. DOS, BIOS and hardware operations are redirected at the lowest practical boundary to SDL3 and portable host services; game logic remains in the reconstructed procedure chain. ## Current status Version 1.1 provides Windows x64 and Linux x86-64 downloads. The Linux binary targets Ubuntu 24.04 or compatible systems with glibc 2.39 or newer and an X11 or Wayland desktop. Other Linux distributions and aarch64 are not release-qualified. See [version 1.1 validation](docs/RELEASE_1_1_VALIDATION.md) for build, test and download smoke-test results. - The reconstructed source is divided between original logic in `src/Original` and platform replacements in `src/SDL`. - The real entry point reaches the original `Setup_Game` procedure; production builds do not substitute a test bootstrap or replacement game loop. - The test suites contain 117 asset-independent headless tests and 148 SDL tests without private game data. Supplying a legal original installation enables 19 additional local asset-integration tests (167 total). - Original title, map, exploration, menus, services, training, combat, save/load and shutdown paths have connected coverage. - A complete manual playthrough and exact presentation/audio fidelity remain uncertified. See [`docs/RUNTIME_STATUS.md`](docs/RUNTIME_STATUS.md).

## Quick start ### Release downloads Download the Windows x64 ZIP or Linux x86-64 tarball from [Releases](https://github.com/Elthial/Crescent-Hawks-Inception-sdl-port/releases). Extract the two runtime files into a writable **copy** of your legally obtained original game installation. Run `CrescentHawksInception.exe` on Windows or `./CrescentHawksInception` on Linux. Saves are written to that copied directory. Linux filenames are case-sensitive; retain the original uppercase data filenames. Both downloads statically link SDL3 and contain no original game data. The Linux download does not require Nix. It uses system display/audio drivers; Ubuntu desktop normally supplies these, while WSL requires WSLg. `CHI_ASSET_DIRECTORY` can instead select another writable copy of the data. ### Linux with Nix Requires Nix with flakes enabled and a legally obtained original game installation. Set `CHI_ORIGINAL_ASSET_DIRECTORY` to that installation, then run: ```sh nix run . ``` On first launch, the launcher copies game data into `${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/crescent-hawks-inception`. Saves remain there across rebuilds. `CHI_ASSET_DIRECTORY` overrides this writable play directory; do not point it at the originals. No game data is bundled. Use `nix build` to build, `nix develop` for a CMake/SDL3 shell, and `nix flake check` for asset-independent tests. `nix run .#integration-tests` requires `CHI_ORIGINAL_ASSET_DIRECTORY` and tests a temporary copy of the data. Pass CTest arguments after `--`; set `CHI_KEEP_TEST_DIRECTORY=1` to keep the build and copied data for debugging. Dependencies are pinned; CMake dependency fetching is disabled. See [Linux test status](docs/LINUX_VALIDATION.md) for validation limits. ### Windows Requirements are Windows, PowerShell, Visual Studio C/C++ build tools and a legally obtained original game installation. CMake/Ninja are taken from Visual Studio; SDL3 is fetched at its pinned checksum unless supplied explicitly. Run the asset-independent Release build and tests: ```powershell ./Build.ps1 -Headless -Configuration Release ``` For local play, put the original data files in `assets/original-game` and run: ```powershell ./Run-Inception.ps1 ``` Or use an installation elsewhere: ```powershell ./Run-Inception.ps1 -OriginalAssetDirectory ../Chinception ``` The direct launcher allows the game to update saves in the selected directory. Use `-Isolated` to play from a private copy under the ignored build directory. The old `Run.ps1` name remains as a compatibility wrapper. ## Minimal runtime package Future GitHub releases build and test both platforms before attaching downloads. See [automated releases](docs/RELEASING.md) for publishing, dry runs and retries. Create a distributable runtime shell with: ```powershell ./Build.ps1 -Configuration Release -Package ``` `build-release/package` contains exactly: ```text CrescentHawksInception.exe CrescentHawksInception.ini ``` SDL3 is linked statically. The package contains no copyrighted game data. `build-release/CrescentHawksInception-1.1.0-SHA256SUMS.txt` records the SHA-256 of both package files and is intentionally kept beside the package directory. With `asset_directory=.`, both files may be copied into an original game installation. A relative or absolute path may instead keep program and data separate. `CHI_ASSET_DIRECTORY` overrides the file for launchers and tests. For the Linux download, build on Ubuntu 24.04 with the SDL Linux build dependencies installed: ```sh cmake -S . -B build-release -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \ -DBUILD_TESTING=ON -DCHI_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS=OFF \ -DCMAKE_DISABLE_FIND_PACKAGE_SDL3=ON cmake --build build-release ctest --test-dir build-release --output-on-failure --parallel 1 cmake --build build-release --target inception-package ``` This uses the checksum-pinned SDL3 source and links it statically. The Linux package contains `CrescentHawksInception` and `CrescentHawksInception.ini`. ## Repository map | Path | Purpose | | --- | --- | | `src/Original` | Readable reconstruction of executable procedures and data | | `src/SDL` | SDL3 and host implementations below DOS/hardware boundaries | | `src/Original/*.h`, `src/SDL/*.h` | Interfaces owned by their respective source domains | | `tests` | Behavioral, integration and preservation checks | | `evidence` | Self-contained annotations, assembly, metadata and research | | `docs` | Current policy, runtime status and focused conversion records | | `tools` | Repository and package validation scripts | | `assets/original-game` | Ignored placeholder for user-supplied original data | The governing rules are in [`docs/PRESERVATION_PLAN.md`](docs/PRESERVATION_PLAN.md), and directory ownership is described in [`docs/SOURCE_LAYOUT.md`](docs/SOURCE_LAYOUT.md). The supported DOS executable hashes are recorded in [`docs/SUPPORTED_VERSIONS.md`](docs/SUPPORTED_VERSIONS.md). Contributions must follow [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md), particularly the original-bug and SDL-boundary rules. Release changes are in [`CHANGELOG.md`](CHANGELOG.md). ## Rights and licensing Project-authored code and excluded reconstructed or third-party material are described in [`LICENSE`](LICENSE), [`LICENSES/README.md`](LICENSES/README.md), [`NOTICE.md`](NOTICE.md), and [`THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). The original executable, game assets and private saves are not included. This is an independent preservation and research project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by the game's publishers or the owners of BattleTech.

nsartem-warcraft-i-decompile-readme-md.text:
# Warcraft: Orcs & Humans — source reconstruction

Evidence-driven decompilation of the DOS release of *Warcraft: Orcs & Humans*
(CD version 1.22h, `WAR.EXE`, Watcom C/C++32 + DOS/4GW).

The repository contains **tools, evidence and reconstructed source only**.
The game itself is never committed; everything is regenerated from your own
copy of the CD dump (`CD_DIC.rar`, Redump/DIC format).

## Quick start

```sh
nix develop                # toolchain: Open Watcom 2, NASM, Python+capstone/unicorn, Ghidra, DOSBox-X
cp /path/to/CD_DIC.rar .
make extract               # CD_DIC.rar -> original/ (every stage hash-verified)
make verify                # symbols + round-trip + C matches + build + tests
make run                   # boot build/war.exe headless, screenshots in build/run/
```

## How it works

1. **Extraction** (`tools/bootstrap.sh`): RAR → data track (MODE1/2352) →
   ISO9660 → `WAR.EXA` (an lh5 archive) → `war.exe`.
2. **Analysis** (`wc1.le`, `wc1.analysis`): LE parsing, then validated
   recursive-descent disassembly seeded by the entry point and every fixup
   target; 97.3% of the code object is decoded instructions/jump tables, the
   remainder verified data-in-code and alignment filler.
3. **Round-trip** (`wc1.emit`, `wc1.roundtrip`): the program is emitted as
   fully symbolic NASM; assembled at the original addresses it is
   byte-identical to the loaded image (99.4% as real instructions).
4. **Rebuild** (`wc1.build`): the same asm, linked with Open Watcom `wlink`
   into a DOS/4GW executable, is load-equivalent to the original (same
   objects, entry, stack, all 8770 fixups) and runs.
5. **Reconstruction**: functions are rewritten in C (`src/`), compiled with
   `wcc386`, and verified with `wc1.match` (identical code and relocation
   targets). Verified functions replace their asm in the build.

See `docs/METHODOLOGY.md` for the evidence/confidence model and verification
tiers, `docs/ANALYST_GUIDE.md` for tools and conventions, and
`docs/REFERENCES.md` for external sources (including the original module
list from the Insider's Guide).

## Status

See `docs/STATUS.md`.

heyhippari-opennomad-readme-md.text:
# OpenNomad

An open-source reimplementation of Omikron: The Nomad Soul, based on reverse engineered behaviour from the original game.

## Disclaimer

This is a reverse engineering project. NO COPYRIGHTED FILES FROM THE ORIGINAL GAME ARE SHARED.

You need a legal copy of the original game in order to run this.

Omikron: The Nomad Soul is the property of Square Enix and Quantic Dream.

## AI Usage Disclaimer

AI was used to help with the reverse engineering process: helping to parse file formats, analyze disassembled functions, help keep track of structs and even find functions Ghidra and OOAnalyzer didn't.

AI was also used for implementation of this SDL3 port. I am primarily a web developer. I do TypeScript, I've done some Rust, quite a bit of Go, a lot of Python. I have very vague notions of C++ and have only practiced C during my teens (as my first programming language aside from typing in BASIC listings on an Amiga 500 before my family got a PC). I still check things, I review code, I guide the agents on architecture, what I'm looking for, what to test against, how to ensure things are implemented correctly based on the reverse engineered specs. But obviously, I am not a C++ developer by trade, so there will no doubt be parts of the code that are dirty, inefficient, badly designed.

## Why ?

The Nomad Soul is one of the first games I played on Windows PCs, back in the late 90s. I remember spending weeks trying to figure out how to mess with the game's files, exploring the various cities, listening to the songs by David Bowie.

It's a janky game, in many respects a bad game, but it's a childhood memory I still cherish. Over the years, the game has developed issues due to technology moving forward.

Every few years, I would remember [a post by David Cage on the late French forum Mayerem](https://web.archive.org/web/20071016020039/http://www.mayerem.com/topic-1158.html#post76174) about open sourcing the game, back in 2006. It never came to pass, but I always wondered "what if".

So I did it myself. Both to finally fulfil the promise David Cage made in 2006 and to ensure the game can keep running on new hardware, different operating systems, and be enjoyable for whoever holds the same weird fondness I have for this questionable piece of software.

## Status

This is EXTREMELY early. I basically started by loading some hardcoded 3DO/3DT files in a scene, and expanded the scope from there.
I am starting with the engine's initialization, because most of the game seems to be script-based. As of the commit this revision of the README is a part of, we have the intro FMV, splash screen and general main menu working, and the introduction of the game works partially. We have also started building an enhancement layer that sits on top of the retail game data and provides small changes intended to make the game feel a bit nicer: smoother transitions, better menu layouts for high resolutions, dynamically cropped introduction FMV, eventually improved subtitle display, etc.

Currently, we can reach the main menu (as well as fix the black background on the game's logo, and improve the layout for larger resolutions of today!), with the intro videos, the splash screen (slightly "improved" with a fade in/out) and music working.

![Screenshot of the modernized main menu](.github/screenshots/title_screen.png)

Next steps: handle the `Quit` menu entry, improve the presentation of the menu a bit more with a very quick fade in/fade out, then start working on the game's introduction.

## How to run

There's not much to run at the moment, but if you're really motivated, follow the instructions in the
[quick start documentation](docs/QuickStart.md).

You can then either copy the original files next to the executable or set an environment variable named
`OPENNOMAD_GAME_DATA_ROOT` to the root folder of the game (where `Runtime.exe` is located).

## Special Thanks

The folks from the original [Mayerem forum (Archive.org mirror)](https://web.archive.org/web/20220121223412/https://www.mayerem.fr/forum.php?sid=8e541bcc0bc6b57fbcf03698ca51995a), for getting the idea of an open source Omikron: The Nomad Soul in my head all these years ago.

[Chevluh](https://github.com/Chevluh/) and Abjab from the Mayerem forum, for the work on [Omikron_Blender_Importer](https://github.com/Chevluh/Omikron_Blender_Importer), documenting some of the 3DO/3DT format.

Quantic Dream and Eidos, for making the game in the first place, and making the little kid I was in 1999 dream about parallel dimensions inside my computer.

missingno7-kegg-recon-readme-md.text:
# Krypton Egg (DOS, 1994) — matching reconstruction

Reconstruct source for `KE.EXE` (Watcom C/C++32 10.0-era, DOS/4GW LE executable) that the historical
toolchain rebuilds into the original bytes — ultimately a byte-identical executable from one WLINK run.

**Status: frozen historical oracle (`historical-exact-clean-v1`).** The cleaned, semantically named source rebuilds
`KE.EXE` byte for byte (SHA-256 `5a465cc7…50b7ee`) from 71 objects with zero raw debt — see docs/freeze.md. Types:
docs/types.md; remaining historical oddities: docs/unresolved.md; SDL3 migration map: docs/porting.md.

## Layout

| path | content |
|---|---|
| `assets/` | original game files (ignored; user supplied) |
| `manifest.json` | the one canonical status file: original identities, functions/regions, status |
| `src/`, `asm/` | canonical reconstructed C / hand-written assembly (only verified material) |
| `tools/` | small deterministic tools (see below) |
| `toolchain/` | `toolchain.json` (pinned installs, hashes, provenance, profiles), `install.py` |
| `docs/` | `evidence.md` (hypothesis register), `bootstrap.md` (lessons from earlier projects) |
| `build/` | everything generated, worker scratch dirs (ignored) |

## Reproduce

```
git clone <repo> && cd <repo>          # any path (compiles run in a short scratch dir, KEGG_TMP or <drive>:\kgtmp)
# put the original game files into assets/ (KE.EXE: 210031 bytes, sha256 below; every verifier refuses any other file)
python toolchain/install.py --verify   # installs, external runners and capstone against their pins; exit 1 on any problem
python tools/validate.py --image --fresh   # FREEZE GATE: every claimed unit/function EXACT, then every object freshly
                                           # compiled (no object cache) and one WLINK run == KE.EXE, raw debt 0
python tests/run.py                    # verifier self-tests (negatives, positives, isolated whole-image negative)
python tools/status.py                 # progress and raw-debt accounting
```

`python tools/validate.py --image` (without `--fresh`) is the fast iteration gate: it reuses
`build/image/objcache` objects whose sidecar metadata re-verifies (source hash, profile, launched tool hashes,
install lock, Watcom `H/` tree hash). Only `--fresh` is used to freeze or to accept a toolchain change.

### External dependencies (all pinned; nothing is fetched automatically)

| dependency | location | pin (full SHA-256) | enforced by |
|---|---|---|---|
| original `KE.EXE` (oracle) | `assets/KE.EXE` (user supplied, ignored) | `5a465cc78d7ef797934f4a95029a278ff10c1ae547ce0cd067eb8c076f50b7ee` (210031 bytes) | `tools/oracle.py` (check.py, image.py fail closed); also `manifest.json` `original` |
| Watcom C/C++32 10.0 GA (compiler `wcc386`, `wlink`, clib3s/math387s/emu387, `wstub`, `H/`) | `C:/tools/watcom-10.0` | tree `5498d143742753b52bdc57c5f76f27d1da224b1996e40ad316fa1a5f681a8157` (2965 files); archive `deaddoomer_WATCOM.zip` `7bf0b04c1d076400bf998a8ad2e2fe1fb7e4d61382b7079b07ed5b282e17a27b` | `install.py --verify`; every launched image (`BINNT/*` stub, `BINB/*` payload, `BIN/wlink.exe`, `BIN/dos4gw.exe`) and each library by `tools/dosrun.py` / `image.py` before use |
| Borland TASM 3.1 (all `game-asm-tasm31` modules) | `C:/tools/watcom-10.0/BIN/TASM.EXE` | `80534cd6a1e2c2b4376ae3f21954c6dbfa77a6998d5e0bf8b8bee6153f3174ea` | `install.py`, `dosrun.py` per run |
| DOSBox-X 2022.09.0 (host of `game-c-ot-dos`: `src/t06.c`, `src/t08.c`) | `C:/tools/dosbox-x/dosbox-x.exe` (or `KEGG_DOSBOX_X`) | `b028a4d328302ea270722dec69f3ec3a10ebf76beba72a51970db33a88df2bf6` | `install.py`, `dosbox.py` / `dosrun.py` per run |
| MS-DOS Player (ReC98 P0281 build; host of TASM/MASM) | `C:/tools/nmlgcdos/msdos.exe` | `f7f6cb0a3e816c5edb13112d327c1bddbf7463fe7bf9a005ca1eb5317751bd02` | `install.py`, `dosrun.py` per run |
| capstone 5.0.7 (py3-none-win_amd64 wheel; disassembly, rel32 decoding) | `build/pylib` (ignored) | tree `65446f83f0aef8bc765ee6c6ff6e4bbe082e34c3343d2b25fbbce3a34463c800` (65 files, `__pycache__` excluded) | `install.py --verify` |
| control installs (not used by the canonical build): Watcom 10.0a, 9.5b, MASM 5.00/5.10/5.10A/6.00, TASM 1.00/1.01/2.00/2.01 | `C:/tools/...` | trees / key files in `toolchain/toolchain.json` | `install.py --verify` (missing = failure) |

Provisioning: the Watcom trees are recreated from their pinned archives with `python toolchain/install.py --install
NAME` (needs `7z`; archives under `C:/tools/download/...`, sources and provenance in `toolchain.json`).
Capstone: `python -m pip install --no-user --target build/pylib capstone==5.0.7` on a networked machine, then
`install.py --verify` checks the tree. DOSBox-X and MS-DOS Player are installed from their upstream releases
and must hash to the pins above. Python 3.10+ (no other packages).

## Toolchain

Historical installs live outside git under `C:/tools` (override `KEGG_TOOLS`), see
`toolchain/toolchain.json`. `python toolchain/install.py --verify` verifies them (tree hashes, key files,
runner and capstone pins; `--quick` skips full trees) and exits 1 on any failure;
`--install NAME` recreates one from its pinned source archive (fatal if the result does not verify).

```
python tools/dosrun.py wcc386 -3s -d2 -s foo.c      # pinned tool, clean environment, every launched image hash-checked
```

## Tools

| command | purpose |
|---|---|
| `python tools/context.py NAME` | worker packet: annotated disassembly, proven declarations, caller usage, best draft |
| `python tools/check.py CAND NAME` | strict verifier for one function (`--all --at A --end B` for a whole TU incl. its data) |
| `python tools/harvest.py DIR...` | check every candidate in worker dirs at once (`--promote`: supervisor only) |
| `python tools/promote.py ...` | single-writer promotion of EXACT functions / asm / units (`--unit`: rolled back unless `validate --image` passes) |
| `python tools/validate.py [--host dosbox] [--image [--fresh]]` | regression gate over everything claimed; `--image` also links the whole EXE; `--fresh` without object cache (freeze) |
| `python tools/image.py --mode canonical [--fresh]` | one WLINK run: canonical sources + explicit raw debt + GA libs -> must equal KE.EXE |
| `python tools/lift.py NAME --refine` | automatic `-d2` decompiler (first drafts; many EXACT) |
| `python tools/tu.py build --range A B` | synthesise a whole translation unit from matched members |
| `python tools/replan.py PLAN.json [--sandbox]` | apply a unit/rename plan atomically (sandbox: full gate in a new unique throwaway copy; renames touching host-pinned sources are refused) |
| `python tools/namefit.py PLAN.json --compile` | rename pre-check: which renames change an importer's object layout |
| `python tools/structure.py src/X.c --out DIR` | verified goto -> structured C rewriting (docs/compiler-notes.md control-flow rules) |
| `python tools/status.py` | progress from manifest.json |
| `tools/le.py`, `omf.py`, `omfwrite.py`, `libscan.py`, `inventory.py`, `tumap.py`, `show.py`, `dosrun.py`, `dosbox.py` | readers/writers and runners |

Docs: `docs/evidence.md` (what is proven), `docs/compiler-notes.md` (Watcom idioms), `docs/grinding.md` and
`docs/units.md` (worker workflows), `docs/bootstrap.md` (lessons from earlier projects).

# D/Generation - TypeScript port of the Amiga AGA release

**[Play it in your browser](https://dux.github.io/d-generation/)** - the GitHub Pages build of `./docs`, no install, keyboard or gamepad.

Made for fast nostalgia re-run, with added unlimited lives, save/restore and an Enhanced 2x view. Amiga lives forever!

| | |
|---|---|
| ![Floor 84, blue scheme](./doc/screenshots/scene85.png) | ![Floor 89, the rooftop](./doc/screenshots/scene145.png) |
| ![Floor 84, red scheme](./doc/screenshots/scene84.png) | ![Floor 87, green scheme](./doc/screenshots/scene118.png) |

Screenshots are rendered by the TypeScript port itself (`bun tools/lockstep/render.ts --scene <n>`), shown at 2x.

This is a 1:1 accurate port of **D/Generation V1.0 for the Amiga AGA** (Robert Cook, conversion by Abersoft, 17 Sep 1993), the full, final release of the game, to plain TypeScript running in the browser.
It is not an emulator.
The original 68000 executable was disassembled routine by routine and rewritten as typed TypeScript state and functions, and every ported routine was checked against the original executable running in a 68000 emulator.
Same rooms, same objects, same AI, same random number sequence, same integer quirks, same game state frame by frame for the same input.

## Status: finished and tested

The port is complete: the whole game runs from the intro and title through all ten floors, the finale with the creature and the dish, and every ending.
It has been played through to the finale in the browser, and every part is checked against the original executable:

* all 139 lockstep scenarios run with no divergence in game state;
* the frame verifier shows the creature's death in scene 122 (the gore splat, the smashed dish, the palette after the red flash) pixel- and colour-identical to the original for every frame of the kill;
* rooms, conversations, inventory, terminals, intro cards, HUD, pause, endings and save states pass their own frame verifiers.

## Why "1:1"

The port is verified in lockstep against the original, not eyeballed.

* A harness (`./tools/m68k/amigaemu.py`, unicorn + stubbed AmigaOS libraries + emulated blitter) runs the original `dgen` executable from the AGA disks.
* `bun run lockstep` steps the original and the TypeScript game with the same input and reports the first frame, global variable or object field that differs.
* The attract demo (3000 main-loop passes, both demos and three attract handoffs) runs with no divergence, both from a native boot and from a state imported from the original.
* 139 scenarios (`./tools/scenarios/`) cover new game, every object class, room exits (including the way out of Derrida's room), lifts, deaths, pickups, conversations, inventory, every terminal, saves, the bomber and the endings, all with no divergence.
* Room drawing is compared pixel by pixel with the original's drawing: 115 of 121 rooms are identical, the other 6 differ only where the original reads past the end of the 100-row city backdrop.
* Conversations, inventory, terminals, intro cards, HUD, pause, endings and save states have their own frame verifiers (`./tools/verify-*.ts`).
* Every ported function starts with a comment naming its address in the original executable, e.g. `// h0:4cbc plyUpdate(): ...`, so any line can be traced back to the 68000 code.
* Integer semantics are kept where they are observable: 8.8 fixed-point positions, byte timers, signedness, wrap-around, truncating division and the order of random calls.

One deliberate difference in drawing: the native renderer draws whole frames, so it does not reproduce the original's dirty-rectangle glitches (objects that moved half a pixel not being redrawn, equal-depth sprites sorting differently in partial redraws).

Full details: `./doc/porting.md` (architecture, rules, verification status, known limits) and `./doc/formats.md` (every original file format).

## Added in this port

Nine additions to the original game, added by Dino Reic ([@dux](https://github.com/dux)).
All live in the browser host (`./src/game/host/worker.ts`); the ported game code only gained two hooks and an option for it (`Game.onLevelRestart`, called after the original Ctrl+R restart, `Game.spawnCreature`, the original creature spawn, and the `newGameCards` option), and plays exactly as the executable without the host.

* **Save / restore anywhere:** F5 / F9, or the Save / Restore buttons in the header, save and restore the full game state at any moment (kept in IndexedDB).
  The original checkpoint saves (Alt+S / Alt+R) still work as before.
* **Unlimited lives:** after every main-loop pass the host sets the lives counter back to 5, so you never get a game over.
* **Restart level button:** asks first, then restarts from the floor checkpoint like the original game's Ctrl+R (the same restart as losing your last life): back to where you arrived on the current floor, with every room of the floor reloaded.
  The key itself is mostly out of reach in a browser, which reloads the page on Ctrl+R.
  During the finale it also gives the escape countdown back (see "15 minutes to escape").
* **Enhanced view:** the Enhanced button doubles the picture to 640x400 with Hyllian's xBR-lv2-noblend on the GPU (WebGL2) before it is scaled to the window.
  It follows 1:1 and 2:1 edges, so diagonal lines get even steps at the doubled resolution, and every new pixel takes one of its neighbours' colours: no blur, no new colours.
  Off by default; the setting is remembered.
* **Story cards on the way in:** the three story cards ("You land on the 80th floor setback...", "The door seals itself behind you...", "Uh...excuse me, but I'm going to need a signature for this, ma'am. Ma'am???") play once per game, just before you enter the first room with a survivor (scene 8, or scene 3 if you go round by scene 43).
  Enter (or any key or button) moves on to the next card, and each card moves on by itself after about 10 seconds.
  The original shows them only in the attract loop, after the title story and the first demo, which a key on the title skips.
* **Survivors' gifts up front:** four survivors hand over an item only for one particular answer: the bomb in scene 23, Michelle's bomb in scene 28, the shield in scene 35 and River's shield in scene 75.
  Here each gift is yours as soon as you start talking to them, once.
* **+Grenade / +Bomb buttons:** one more grenade (up to 99) or bomb (up to 9) per click.
* **15 minutes to escape:** after the dream (the eyes and cross) and Derrida's room, the original gives you a hidden countdown of about 100 seconds to reach the exit control room, scene 121, before it cuts to the jet-pack; here it is about 15 minutes.
  Restart level while it runs, or any time after it stopped until you fry the creature (the creature out in scene 121, a death's jet-pack cut, the ending text), gives you the whole 15 minutes again from where you arrived on the floor.
* **The creature waits in scene 121:** the original shows it only on the entry that stops the countdown; here it is back every time you enter the room until the dish fries it.

## How each part was ported

| Part | Original | Ported as | Where | Checked by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Game logic (main loop, objects, AI, collisions, timers) | SAS/C 68000 code in `dgen` (hunk h0) | Disassembled routine by routine and rewritten as typed TypeScript state and functions, each tagged with its `h0:` address; one module per object class | `./src/game/core/`, `./src/game/actors/` | `bun run lockstep`, 139 scenarios |
| Random numbers | `h0:e7f4`, two byte LCGs in one word | Same generator, including the original's high-byte read quirk and the order of calls | `./src/game/core/random.ts` | lockstep (seed is compared) |
| Levels | `DATA/L1..L10.SCN`, `MAPMTX0..2.DAT` room packs | Decoded to one editable JSON5 file per floor; rooms build their own runtime grid, level data stays read-only | `./levels/`, `./src/formats/level.ts` | `bun run extract:levels` round trip, byte for byte |
| Sprites | `aga/*.aga` shape trees of bitplane frames with a mask plane | Atlas PNG per bank (grey = palette index, alpha = mask) plus JSON sets and frame offsets; the blitter draw and horizontal mirror (`h10:16`, `h10:262`) are reimplemented on indexed pixels | `./assets/sprites/`, `./src/formats/shape.ts`, `./src/game/render/gfx.ts` | extractor reads every file back and compares it with the original decode |
| Room decoration (delta images) | `DATA/DLTSET*.DAT` run-length command streams | Commands pre-rendered to grey + alpha atlases with draw offsets; colour `0xfc` still shows the backdrop | `./assets/deltas/`, `./src/formats/delta.ts` | `bun run verify:aga-rooms` |
| Room drawing | `h0:1250` | Same order: tiles, floor lines, back deltas, walls with joins, tall wall tops, drops and lines, front deltas; clipped at row 181 | `./src/game/render/room.ts` | 115 of 121 rooms pixel-identical |
| Object drawing | Dirty-rectangle redraw with depth sorting and wall occlusion | Same ordering and occlusion, but whole frames are drawn every time | `./src/game/render/objects.ts` | `bun run verify:aga-frames` |
| Pictures and backdrop | LZW `*.vim` (8 bitplanes), `BACK1.DAT`, CD32 keyboard and pad menu in hunk 9 | Unpacked to grey PNGs of palette indexes, decoded in the browser so indexes stay indexes | `./assets/images/`, `./src/formats/png.ts` | extractor read-back |
| Palettes and effects | `DATA/*.PAL` (6-bit), palette scripts `h0:b0dc` | `palettes.json`; room schemes swap colours 32..79, flashes and scripts are ported code | `./assets/palettes.json`, `./src/game/core/effects.ts` | lockstep, frame verifiers |
| Font and text | Glyphs in shape set 36 of `b1.aga`, advance table `g:3b03`, strings in the data hunk | Glyphs come from the sprite atlas, word wrap and `\|c` colour codes are ported, strings are TypeScript constants | `./src/game/render/gfx.ts`, `./src/game/ui/talk/text.ts` | `./tools/verify-talk-frames.ts`, `./tools/verify-ui-frames.ts` |
| Sound effects | `amiga.eff` (raw signed 8-bit), sample table `h11:45e6`, sound table `h11:44f6`, Paula driver `h0:1551a` / `h10:37f6` | One WAV per sample; a WebAudio driver keeps Paula's four channels, first-free-channel allocation, stereo sides and the `3546895 / period` rate; sounds 33 and 48 loop | `./assets/sounds/`, `./src/formats/sound.ts`, `./src/game/host/audio.ts` | extractor read-back |
| Music | OctaMED `dgen.mod` and `dgen2.mod`, started by `h0:77ec`, stopped when `amiga.eff` is loaded | Rendered once with libopenmpt (chiptune3) to Opus and looped; the game emits `music` events from the same phases: `dgen` on the first title pass (ends after the module's tick length), none in demos and play, `dgen2` in the good ending | `./assets/music/`, `./src/audio/music.ts`, `./src/game/core/game.ts` | title timing via lockstep |
| Attract demos | `DATA/DEMO50.SEQ`, `DEMO52.SEQ` | JSON direction and button records, replayed by the ported demo player | `./assets/demos/`, `./src/game/core/demo.ts` | 3000-pass attract run, no divergence |
| UI (title, intro, HUD, pause, conversations, inventory, terminals, endings, CD32 menu) | Game code in h0 | Ported like the game logic | `./src/game/ui/` | `./tools/verify-ui-*.ts`, `./tools/verify-talk-frames.ts` |
| Input | Amiga raw key codes, CD32 pad, on-screen keyboard for prompts | Browser keys sent as raw codes, gamepad mapped to the pad; the host drives the on-screen keyboard when you type | `./src/game/core/input.ts`, `./src/game/host/input.ts`, `./src/game/host/typing.ts` | scenarios replay raw key and joystick events |
| Timing | PAL vblank and CIA interrupts, synchronous busy waits | Game runs in a Worker on shared memory, one call per 20 ms tick, sleeping on Atomics so the original waits run unchanged | `./src/game/host/worker.ts` | lockstep under the harness tick model |
| Saves | Checkpoint save of nonvolatile items, `DATA/DGEN.CFG` | Checkpoints in localStorage, `config.json`; save states (F5 / F9) added on top in IndexedDB | `./src/game/ui/save.ts`, `./src/game/host/host.ts` | `./tools/verify-snapshot.ts` |

## The game

You are a jet-pack courier delivering a package to Genoq Biolabs in Singapore, 2021.
You land on the 80th floor and the building seals itself behind you: the security system has gone haywire and Genoq's bioweapons (A/Generation, B/Generation and C/Generation) are loose.
Fight your way up ten floors of isometric rooms, solve door, switch, laser and teleporter puzzles, rescue the trapped staff and find Dr. Derrida, the head of the special operations lab.

D/Generation was first published by Mindscape in 1991 for MS-DOS, then for Amiga OCS/ECS and Atari ST (1992), Amiga AGA and CD32 (1993).
The AGA executable is the CD32 code base: 256-colour graphics, the CD32 pad menu and the on-screen keyboard for terminal prompts.

## Play

```sh
bun install
bun dev          # development page: Play, plus room / sprite / delta viewers
bun run build    # GitHub Pages site into ./docs (game.html as index.html)
bun run preview  # serve ./docs locally with the COOP/COEP headers
```

The game runs in a module Worker on shared memory, so it needs cross-origin isolation; `bun dev` sends the headers and the Pages build adds them with a service worker (`./src/pages/coi-sw.js`).

### Controls

* Arrow keys or keypad move; held arrows combine into diagonals.
* All other keys are passed through as Amiga raw key codes, so the original keyboard controls work as in the manual.
* Gamepad: stick or d-pad moves, button 0 fires, button 1 uses.
* Terminal prompts: just type; the host drives the CD32 on-screen keyboard for you (Enter = RET, Backspace = DEL).
* Space (or gamepad button 1): the laser, which bounces off walls and triggers switches.
* T (or gamepad button 0): throw a grenade the way you face; you need grenades picked up on the way (S shows how many).
* Enter: talk to the survivor in front of you; up / down picks an answer, Enter takes it, and the conversation goes on until you leave it with Esc (or gamepad button 0).
* U: the inventory; left / right picks an item, Enter (or gamepad button 1) uses it, Esc or U closes it.
  Only items you have are shown: bomb, freezer, shield, barrier and the package; a placed bomb blasts doors.
* Alt+S / Alt+R: the original checkpoint save and restore (kept in localStorage).
* F5 / F9, or the Save / Restore buttons: save states (kept in IndexedDB).
* Restart level button (the original Ctrl+R): back to where you arrived on the current floor, after a confirmation.
* +Grenade / +Bomb buttons: one more grenade or bomb.
* Enhanced button: twice the pixel density (xBR-lv2-noblend) on or off.
* Ctrl+B: the original CD32 menu.

### Passwords

The terminal in scene 23 (building floor 81) asks for a user name and passcode; Seth, the survivor in scene 4, gives them away:

* Username: `Seth`
* Password: `Ostrich`

The entrance-code terminal in scene 82 (building floor 84) has no fixed password.
Its code is one of the four horsemen, `War`, `Death`, `Pestilence` or `Famine`, picked when the title screen last ran, and John of Maryland in scene 84 tells you which one ("I am the bringer of ...").
In this port a game started right after loading the page uses `Death`; a game started after going back to the title screen uses `War`.

The exit control terminal in scene 121 (building floor 89) needs no typing; it only shows "Passcode 'REGENERATION' has been entered.  Exit door is now open."

### Hints

The guaranteed bombs come from survivors: the one in scene 23 (building floor 81) and Michelle in scene 28 (building floor 82).
Shields come from the survivor in scene 35 (building floor 82) and River in scene 75 (building floor 85, "some sort of personal barrier").
Each of them stays seated until their room is secured and they can see you; then Enter starts the conversation and the gift is yours (see "Added in this port").
In the original you only get it for one answer (for River `No.`, then `No, you aren't fat.`, then `OK!  OK!  You're fat and ugly!`); that answer still adds one more.
One more bomb is in the plain cubicle of scene 39: cubicle items are rolled from a fixed seed here, so it is always a bomb.
Restart level reloads the floor and with it the survivors.

## Repository layout

* `./src/game/core/`: game state, boot and main loop, input, floors and rooms, object system, collisions, timers, random, messages, palette effects.
* `./src/game/actors/`: one module per original object class (player, doors, lasers, lifts, teleporters, survivors, bioweapons, Derrida, ...).
* `./src/game/render/`: room and object drawing with the original's ordering and wall occlusion.
* `./src/game/ui/`: title, intro, attract, pause, saves, endings, conversations, inventory, terminals, CD32 menus.
* `./src/game/host/`: browser host (Worker, keyboard and gamepad, WebAudio, saves).
* `./levels/floor01.json5` .. `floor10.json5`: the ten floors as editable JSON5, round-trip checked byte for byte against the original `L1..L10.SCN` packs (schema in `./levels/README.md`).
* `./assets/`: graphics, palettes, sounds and music converted from the original files by `bun run extract:assets`.
* `./amiga/adf/`, `./amiga/aga/`: the two original AGA disk images and their unpacked files, the source of truth; git-ignored, not in this repository (bring your own, see below).
* `./tools/`: 68000 harness, disassembly kit, lockstep runner, scenario runner and frame verifiers.

## Get the original game

The original Amiga release can be found on these archive and abandonware sites:

* [Lemon Amiga - D/Generation AGA](https://www.lemonamiga.com/game/d-generation-aga) (the release this port is based on)
* [Lemon Amiga - D/Generation OCS/ECS](https://www.lemonamiga.com/game/d-generation)
* [Lemon Amiga - D/Generation CD32](https://www.lemonamiga.com/game/d-generation-cd32)
* [Lemon Amiga - original manual](https://www.lemonamiga.com/doc/d-generation/472)
* [Hall of Light - the Amiga games database](https://hol.abime.net/256) (more entries: [3557](https://hol.abime.net/3557), [257](https://hol.abime.net/257))
* [Free Game Downloads (mosw) - D/Generation AGA](https://free-game-downloads.mosw.com/abandonware/amiga/games_d_e/d_generation_aga.html)
* [GamesNostalgia - D/Generation](https://gamesnostalgia.net/game/dgeneration)
* [OpenRetro - D/Generation (Amiga)](https://openretro.org/amiga/d-generation)
* [WHDLoad install by JOTD](https://whdload.de/games/DGeneration.html) (hard-disk installer for the ECS/AGA/CD32 versions)
* [My Abandonware - D/Generation (DOS)](https://www.myabandonware.com/game/d-generation-14l)
* [Abandonware France - D/Generation (DOS, credits)](https://www.abandonware-france.org/ltf_abandon/ltf_jeu.php?id=321)
* [Internet Archive - D/Generation (DOS, playable in the browser)](https://archive.org/details/msdos_D-Generation_1991)

Background and reviews: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D/Generation), [MobyGames](https://www.mobygames.com/game/1274/dgeneration/), [Amiga Power 32 review of the CD32 version (Amiga Magazine Rack)](https://amr.abime.net/review_1427).

## Credits and attribution

D/Generation is the work of its original authors; this repository only translates their program to another language.

Game credits, as shown on the game's own credits screen (`DATA/CRED.VIM`):

| Role | Name |
|---|---|
| Programming | Robert Cook (now Veda Hlubinka-Cook) |
| Programming | Jim Brown |
| Programming | John Jones-Steele |
| Title music | Sean Gugler |
| Additional graphics | Vicki Sidley, Tansi Brooks, Steve Leney |

* Original design: Robert Cook, who first built the game as *D-Generation* for the 128K Apple IIe in 1989-1990 (never released).
* Amiga conversion: Abersoft ("Conversion by Abersoft Sep 17 1993" in the executable).
* Publisher: Mindscape, Inc. (US) and Mindscape International (Europe).
* Copyright line in the executable: "Copyright 1993 Robert Cook and Mindscape".

Tools and libraries used by the port:

* [amitools](https://github.com/cnvogelg/amitools) (`xdftool`) to unpack the ADF disk images.
* [Unicorn](https://www.unicorn-engine.org/) and [Capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/) for the 68000 harness and disassembly.
* [chiptune3](https://github.com/DrSnuggles/chiptune) / libopenmpt to render the original `dgen.mod` and `dgen2.mod` tracks.
* [xBR-lv2-noblend](https://github.com/libretro/glsl-shaders/blob/master/xbr/shaders/xbr-lv2-noblend.glsl) by Hyllian (MIT) for the Enhanced view, ported to WebGL2 in `./src/game/host/xbr.ts`.
* [Vite](https://vite.dev/), [Bun](https://bun.sh/), [TypeScript](https://www.typescriptlang.org/), [json5](https://json5.org/).

## Rights

D/Generation, its code, graphics, levels, text, sound and music are copyright Robert Cook and Mindscape and their successors in interest.
This is a non-commercial preservation and study project with no affiliation to the rights holders.
If you own rights to the game and want something changed or removed, please open an issue.

# EdMap

A Rust + egui rebuild of [Jeff Rabenhorst's EdMap v1.40](https://doomwiki.org/wiki/EdMap)
(1994 — DOOM/DOOM II/HERETIC map editor for DOS).

Written from scratch in 2026, working from the public DOOM WAD format spec,
the original `EDMAPSYS.EXE` binary's strings table, and the EdMap.txt
documentation file. Aims for visual + behavioral fidelity to the DOS original
with modern conveniences (native file pickers, Save warnings, Undo, real
texture decoding) layered on top.

![EdMap editing E1M1](screenshots/editor-layout-E1M1.png)

Most original menu items are now wired. Recent additions: a software/GL 3D walk-around
view, sector style clipboard, tag-line tool, and an "Enhance map" combo cleaner.

## Differences from the original

Intentional departures, in rough order of how often they'll bite you:

- **No DOOM engine bundled.** "Play map" shells out to a configured external
  port (gzdoom, dsda-doom, etc.) — set the path + arg template under
  File (map) → Test map settings. Internal nodes-builder for "Build & save"
  is still placeholder; a node builder runs at PWAD-build time when needed.
- **3D view is editor-side, not a play preview.** Q toggles a fly-camera with
  textured walls/floors/ceilings and thing markers, useful for spotting
  height/texture mistakes without leaving the editor.
- **No 16-bit XMS / disk swapping.** Modern OSes have plenty of RAM.
- **Native file dialogs** via `rfd` instead of the home-brewed in-app file
  picker. Faster, integrates with macOS/Linux/Windows file systems.
- **No `MOUSEPIC.DAT`** — the OS owns the cursor.
- **Auto-snap differences.** Drag uses a residual accumulator so very slow
  drags still register motion across frames; the original used pixel-step.
- **Stairs and Polygon don't weld duplicate vertices.** A node builder
  cleans this up at PWAD-build time, but the in-memory geometry is denser
  than EdMap's would be. A future `weld_duplicates` pass will fix it.

## Reverse-engineering notes

`specs/001-edmap-nextgen/re-notes.md` documents the radare2 + DOSBox-X
workflow and what we've found in `EDMAPSYS.EXE`:

- Borland Turbo Pascal MZ build, single `.text` segment carries code +
  Pascal length-prefixed strings. DGROUP base ≈ vaddr `0xCD8E`.
- The LineDef-check function chain: `fcn.0001584c` (iter scaffold) →
  `fcn.00016248` (per-line inspector) → `fcn.00015d9e` (error display).
- The exact "long LineDef" warning threshold is still unverified — our
  approximation is 1024 units. To pin it precisely, run EdMap in DOSBox-X
  with a stub PWAD and bisect.

## Original credits

EdMap v1.40 — Jeff Rabenhorst (araya@wam.umd.edu), 1994. Distributed free,
no registration. The original is included in this repo as `EDMAP.EXE` and
`EDMAPSYS.EXE` for RE reference; full source has never been released.

DOOM, DOOM II, and HERETIC are trademarks of id Software / Raven Software.
This rebuild produces PWADs in the standard format and is not affiliated
with id, Raven, ZeniMax, or Bethesda.

## License

The Rust rebuild source code in `src/` is dedicated to the public domain
(unless overridden by a future LICENSE file). Bundled asset TTFs carry
their own licenses — see `src/assets/README.md`. The original 1994 EdMap
binaries are unmodified and redistributed under their original
"completely free; no registration required" terms.

# Dungeon Keeper (`KEEPER.EXE`) — Full Reconstructed Source Repository

This repository contains the complete reverse-engineered source reconstruction of Bullfrog Productions' **Dungeon Keeper** (`KEEPER.EXE`, 1997 DOS/4GW release), generated using **REA `6.5.0`** and **Ghidra `12.1.4`** on `server-taller`.

## Summary Statistics

| Metric | Value |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Original Binary** | `/home/merlin/Dungeon Keeper/KEEPER.EXE` (`1,923,995` bytes, Watcom C/C++ DOS/4GW `LE`) |
| **Relocated ELF32 Image** | `/home/merlin/Dungeon Keeper/re/KEEPER.elf` (`1,638,548` bytes, `45,949` internal fixups + `4,368` `.symtab` `STT_FUNC` entries) |
| **Entry Point (VA)** | `0x000f4448` (`Obj 1 + 0xe4448`) |
| **Recovered Functions** | **4418** decompiled procedures (`0x00010000` – `0x001447a0`) |
| **Recovered Defined Strings** | **7692** string literals (`0x00160000` – `0x0019a000`) |
| **Reconstructed Source Modules** | **90** `.cpp` translation units (**85/85** original Bullfrog `.cpp` files + `4` `bflib/` modules + `1` `rt/` module, all non-empty) |
| **Tracked Global Symbols** | **2500** global data/BSS symbols (`0x00160000` – `0x00402024`) |

## Repository Structure

- [`include/`](./include/) — Reconstructed C/C++ headers:
  - [`dk_types.h`](./include/dk_types.h) — Fixed-width primitive types & Watcom conventions
  - [`dk_structs.h`](./include/dk_structs.h) — Core engine structs (`Thing`, `Coord3d`, `Packet`, `CommandDesc`, `SlabMap`, `TbSprite`, `TbNetworkSession`)
  - [`dk_globals.h`](./include/dk_globals.h) — Global `.data_obj3` and `.bss_obj3` variable declarations with exact virtual addresses
  - [`dk_functions.h`](./include/dk_functions.h) — Master function prototype declarations across all 4418 procedures
- [`src/`](./src/) — Reconstructed C/C++ translation units (`85` original Bullfrog `.cpp` modules + [`src/bflib/`](./src/bflib/) + [`src/rt/`](./src/rt/)) containing all **4418** decompiled functions with recovered `LbErrorLog(__FILE__, __LINE__, msg)` annotations
- [`docs/`](./docs/) — Technical reverse-engineering documentation:
  - [`ARCHITECTURE.md`](./docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) — Memory layout, module map, and call-graph architecture
  - [`SUBSYSTEM_MULTIPLAYER.md`](./docs/SUBSYSTEM_MULTIPLAYER.md) — Deep dive into `frontnet.cpp`, `packet.cpp`, and `LbNetwork_*` lockstep networking
  - [`SUBSYSTEM_GRAPHICS.md`](./docs/SUBSYSTEM_GRAPHICS.md) — Deep dive into `setup.cpp`, `engine3.cpp`, `draw.cpp`, `column.cpp`, `ceiling.cpp`, `light.cpp`, `ssprite.cpp`, and `eyelens.cpp`
  - [`DATA_FORMATS.md`](./docs/DATA_FORMATS.md) — Binary specifications of `DATA/*.DAT`, `*.TAB`, `levels/MAP*.*`, and `SAVE/CONTINUE.SAV`
  - [`FUNCTION_INDEX.md`](./docs/FUNCTION_INDEX.md) — Complete searchable table of all 4418 functions
- [`catalog/`](./catalog/) — Raw machine-readable REA + Ghidra JSON/JSONL catalogs (`functions.jsonl`, `procedures.json`, `strings.json`, `module_map.json`, `globals_map.json`, `source_file_xrefs.json`)

## Native Compilation & Execution

The repository includes a native hybrid recompiler runtime that executes the original 32-bit game logic, level engine, and renderer directly on modern operating systems without DOSBox emulation:

- **Linux (x86 / x86_64 with multilib)**: `build/keeper_linux32`
- **Windows 10 / 11 (Win32 / WoW64)**: `build/keeper_win32.exe`

### Building from Source

```bash
# Build both Linux 32-bit and Windows 32-bit executables
make all

# Or build individually:
make linux   # builds build/keeper_linux32
make win32   # cross-compiles build/keeper_win32.exe with i686-w64-mingw32
```

### Running the Native Engine

#### On Ubuntu Server / Linux Workstation

```bash
# Automated headless validation (dumps 120 frames to build/frames/):
make validate

# Direct-to-level headless test:
./build/keeper_linux32 --game-dir "/home/merlin/Dungeon Keeper" --level 1 --max-frames 120 --dump-frames build/frames -nosound
```

#### On Windows 10 Workstation

Copy `build/keeper_win32.exe` to your local machine (e.g. into your Dungeon Keeper game directory):
```powershell
.\keeper_win32.exe --game-dir "C:\Games\Dungeon Keeper"
```

### Architecture & Recompiled Function Detours

- [`runtime/keeper_runtime.c`](./runtime/keeper_runtime.c) handles binary segment mapping (`0x00010000..0x00450000`), dynamic x86 `__watcall` and `__cdecl` bridge thunks (including callee stack pop `ret $N`), and redirects Bullfrog BFLib low-level DOS interrupts/hardware calls to modern standard C runtime and OS graphics/input APIs.
- [`runtime/recompiled_modules.cpp`](./runtime/recompiled_modules.cpp) compiles native C++ modules from `src/` (e.g., `packet.cpp`, `ssprite.cpp`) and hot-patches their function addresses directly over the original binary, enabling progressive replacement of decompiled C++ routines while maintaining full binary compatibility and testability.
